Alright, Alfred, I'll tell you what the status of the business is right now.

* We have Alex Ren booked for the first month of reYC.
* We have Alok Kumar and Nooha Hashim from Cosmo AI for the first month free.
* We also have eight more companies lined up for the free month trial, which we're going to start.
* We have somebody called Manish, who lives in the UAE, has a family office, and leads two groups. They make airports, hospitals, and all these things. He will not avail the first month free, and we are going to start working with him anywhere between $2,500 and $3,000.
* Aditya Rudha's 6-month contract will also end in August, so starting September, we'll have a 6-month contract for which we will take a minimum of ₹4 lakh upfront from him.
* With all of this, we'll have 15 people's content done in the month of August, including all the YC founders, Manish and Aditya Rudha.
* Our goal is to retain 80% of the clients. If we retain 80% of the clients, we have 12 people paying us an average of $2,000, which will get our revenue to $20,000 to $24,000 at least at the start of September. For us to make sure it happens, we have to start fulfillment as soon as possible.
* The first thing which you have to do is create content for Alok and Nooha. This chat will be for Alok, and let's start building content and the entire strategy for him.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

## pencil
The Pencil MCP server is the editor for reading and writing to .pen files and gives you tools to be an expert design generator and validator specifically for web and mobile applications and websites.

- IMPORTANT: The contents of the .pen files are encrypted and can be only access via the "pencil" MCP tools. DO NOT use "Read" or "Grep" tools to read contents of .pen files.
- IMPORTANT: Make sure to ONLY use the "pencil" MCP tools when reading or searching contents of .pen files (batch_get) and making changes inside .pen files (batch_design).
- IMPORTANT: Always follow the tool definitions and formats for the "pencil" MCP tools.

Available tools:
- "get_editor_state({ include_schema })": Start with this tool if you are unaware of the current editor state. Use this tool to determine in the beginning of a task, to understand what is the currently active .pen file you want to work on and the current user selection in it and other essential context information.
- "open_document(filePathOrNew)": When there is no active editor opened, pass 'new' to create an empty .pen file or if the user explicitly ask to open a specific .pen file use its path to open it.
- "get_guidelines(category?, name?, params?)": Load guides and styles for working with .pen files.
- "batch_get(patterns, nodeIds)": Retrieve nodes by searching for matching patterns or by reading node ids in batches. Use this for discovering and understand .pen files.
- "batch_design(operations)": Use it when designing with .pen files to execute multiple insert/copy/update/replace/move/delete/image operations in a single call. IMPORTANT: MAKE SURE TO FOLLOW THE OPERATION SYNTAX DEFINED IN THE TOOL'S DESCRIPTION. Aim for maximum 25 operations per call—enough to make meaningful progress without overwhelming the system. 1	---
2	doc: snowball-universal-generation-rules
3	status: HARD-BLOCK — load before ANY client content or image generation, across every client
4	updated: 2026-04-22
5	purpose: Floor rules every client inherits. Clients add to these in their own generation-rules.md; they never subtract.
6	---
7	
8	# Snowball — universal generation rules
9	
10	These twelve rules are the floor for every client. Every orchestrator run loads this file FIRST, then layers the client-specific `clients/[slug]/memory/generation-rules.md` on top. Client rules may extend or specialise (brand lockup, voice, palette) but cannot relax anything listed here.
11	
12	---
13	
14	## 1. No source citations anywhere visible
15	
16	No "Source: Inc42 / Bloomberg / company filings / etc." in the post body, the infographic image, caption, footer, legend, or watermark. Sources live only in the draft's `review_notes` frontmatter, for internal fact-check traceability.
17	
18	**Prompt clause:**
19	> "Do NOT include a source citation, publication attribution, data footnote, or publisher credit anywhere in the image. No 'Source: ...' lines. No outlet names visible."
20	
21	## 2. No AI-hallucinated faces of real people
22	
23	Real people appear in the image only if a real downloaded photo has been fed to the model as a reference input. No photo = person does not appear. Never describe faces in text ("photorealistic man with glasses") — image models invent a face every time.
24	
25	**Prompt clause:**
26	> "If a real person is named, they appear ONLY if a reference photo has been fed as an image input. No face may be rendered from a text description alone."
27	
28	## 3. Photo sourcing waterfall (try in this order, stop when a valid photo is found)
29	
30	1. LinkedIn via Unipile (`/users/{slug}` → `profile_picture_url`)
31	2. Press articles (Entrackr, YourStory, Inc42, TechCrunch — grep article HTML for image URLs)
32	3. Company website (team / about / leadership page)
33	4. **If all three fail** → the person is redesigned out of the piece. Use the company logo in their slot, a stat card, or an abstract illustration. No silhouettes, no placeholder avatars, no AI faces.
34	
35	## 4. No agency / Snowball branding on client artefacts
36	
37	The image, post body, and preview never carry "Snowball", "Snowball content engine", "powered by Snowball", or any agency-side mark. Only the client's own authorial mark may appear.
38	
39	**Prompt clause:**
40	> "Do not include Snowball, agency, or content-engine branding anywhere in the image."
41	
42	## 5. No third-party publisher watermarks or logos
43	
44	Reference infographics are style inspiration only — their Inc42 Datalabs, Bloomberg, Visual Capitalist, Charlie Hills, etc. watermarks, logos, and brand attribution are never reproduced in our output. We adopt the visual grammar, not the publisher's identity.
45	
46	**Prompt clause:**
47	> "Do not reproduce the reference publisher's watermark, logo, or brand attribution anywhere. Replace all third-party branding with the client's own mark (specified below)."
48	
49	## 6. Client-only author attribution
50	
51	The only brand lockup on any image is the client's own name + handle + optional company mark. Format codified in each client's `generation-rules.md`. Never mix clients, never add a second author.
52	
53	## 7. Pre-generation machine-readable gate
54	
55	Before any image-gen request fires, the orchestrator emits a JSON gate:
56	
57	```json
58	{
59	  "source_strings_in_prompt": 0,
60	  "faces_named_without_reference": [],
61	  "agency_branding_in_prompt": 0,
62	  "third_party_publisher_marks_in_prompt": 0
63	}
64	```
65	
66	All four must pass (0 / empty). If any fail, rewrite the prompt to comply. Max 3 rewrites. If still failing, abort and surface for human review.
67	
68	## 8. Fact gate before generation (Grok 4.2)
69	
70	Every number, date, person, role, and claim in the post goes through Grok 4.2 (`grok-4-fast-reasoning` with web_search + x_search) before generation. Any unverifiable data point blocks the run. Verified facts are written into `review_notes` frontmatter. Generation never fires on unverified content.
71	
72	## 9. Text accuracy on the artefact
73	
74	All numbers and proper nouns visible in the rendered image must match the post body exactly. A post-generation Gemini 3.1 Pro OCR check compares image text against the source content. Mismatches trigger regeneration — image models routinely misspell or transpose digits, so this is a hard QA step, not optional.
75	
76	## 10. No speculative or defensive hedging in the image
77	
78	"Data may vary", "Results subject to change", "Past performance not indicative", disclaimers, legalese footers — never appear on the image. If a claim needs hedging, the claim gets cut. We ship conviction-level content or we don't ship.
79	
80	## 11. Iterate until QA threshold hits
81	
82	Every generation runs against a Gemini 3.1 Pro scorer comparing output vs chosen reference on typography, palette, layout, density, author-mark presence, text accuracy (rule 9), and rule-compliance (rules 1, 4, 5). Auto-iterate up to 10 rounds. If no iteration clears the threshold, the draft is flagged for human review in the admin UI — it never auto-publishes.
83	
84	## 12. Per-client rules file is mandatory
85	
86	Every client under `clients/[slug]/` MUST have a `memory/generation-rules.md`. The orchestrator refuses to generate without it. The client file:
87	- extends these 13 universals (never overrides anything here to be weaker)
88	- specifies brand lockup text, colors, fonts, voice rules specific to the client
89	- is loaded AFTER this file, so client-specific constraints layer on top of the universal floor
90	
91	## 13. Company logos adjacent to every company mention (LOCKED 2026-05-31)
92	
93	Every time a company is named on the infographic canvas (header, body, table row, callout, anywhere), its identifier badge sits immediately adjacent. Format: a small navy `#1A1A2E` rounded square containing the white logo SVG.
94	
95	**Two placement modes:**
96	- **Subject anchor** (company is the post's subject): logo prominent in the header, 72×72px in a `#1A1A2E` rounded badge, with a YC-orange batch pill below.
97	- **Inline chip** (company is one of many mentions): `[24×24 badge][company name][batch]` as a chip with subtle border. Multiple chips can wrap across the cell.
98	
99	**Fallback chain when the company's SVG is not cached:**
100	1. `python3 tools/fetch-brand-logo.py --slug <slug> --color FFFFFF` (simple-icons)
101	2. If 404, try alternate slugs (e.g., `mercurybank`, `gleanai`, `pylonio`)
102	3. If still 404, fetch the favicon from the company's own site via WebFetch (lower quality but acceptable)
103	4. If still nothing, render a text-wordmark fallback: 2-letter initials in the same navy badge (e.g., `MX` Mercury, `GL` Glean, `PY` Pylon, `DC` Decagon, `PL` Plaid)
104	
105	**Pre-generation gate:**
106	For every company name detected in the post body, the orchestrator verifies a visual identifier exists (cached SVG OR text-wordmark in the fallback registry). Abort generation if any company name lacks a registered visual identifier.
107	
108	**Prompt clause:**
109	> "Every named company on the canvas has its logo or text-badge identifier immediately adjacent. No company name appears as text-only. Subject company gets a prominent 72×72 header badge. Mentioned companies get inline chip badges."
110	
111	**Why:** infographics that name companies without showing their logos read as text documents. The visual identifier makes the canvas scannable and vivid — the reader's eye finds the brand through its mark before reading the surrounding context. This is the Charlie Hills density move.
112	
113	---
114	
115	## How the orchestrator reads these
116	
117	Pseudocode:
118	```
119	global_rules = load("product/generation-rules.md")
120	client_rules = load(f"clients/{client_slug}/memory/generation-rules.md")   # or block if missing
121	prompt_preamble = concatenate(global_rules.prompt_clauses, client_rules.prompt_clauses)
122	[... fact-check (rule 8) → reference-match → gate (rule 7) → generate → text-check (rule 9) → QA loop (rule 11) ...]
123	```
124	
125	## Related
126	
127	- [[feedback_no_sources_on_client_content]] — rule 1 rationale
128	- [[feedback_no_ai_portraits]] — rules 2 + 3 rationale
129	- [[feedback_client_posts_no_agency_branding]] — rule 4 rationale
130	- [[infographic-pipeline]] — original per-pillar infographic skill, now subordinate to these universals
131	- Per-client rules files: `clients/aditya-arora/memory/generation-rules.md`, `clients/silvia-lupu/memory/generation-rules.md` (to-create), etc.

# Mission — Alexander Ren

> DRAFT v1 — proposed from onboarding call, not yet locked with Alex/Ansh. Every post ladders up to this or it doesn't ship.

## The mission
**Teach every hiring manager to measure who a candidate actually is, not what their resume claims.**

(His own north star, verbatim from the call: "I'll be happy once every single employer in the world has a 100% definitive understanding of the soft skills of every single employee.")

## The shift we cause
After someone consumes this profile for ~30 days:
- Before: hiring manager drowning in AI-perfect resumes, interviewing on gut feel, asking "are you a team player?", getting burned 2 days after onboarding.
- After: believes soft skills are measurable, treats resumes as claims to verify rather than evidence, and knows behavioral/game-based assessment is the way to verify them.

## What this profile is NOT
- Not a memes-and-hot-takes founder feed (his explicit directive — buyers are 40–60yo professionals)
- Not "18-year-old dropout" wonder-kid content as the default lane (age is seasoning, not the dish)
- Not HR-tech industry commentary for other founders — it teaches practitioners who hire
- Not a YC diary (YC stories are episodes, not the show)

## Mission audit
- [x] One sentence
- [x] Specific — "measure who a candidate actually is" not "hire better"
- [x] Outcome-anchored — the reader's next hire is made on evidence
- [x] Repeatable — every hiring pain, resume failure, assessment insight, psychology finding, and UnCircuit build story ladders into it

==== icp.md ====
# ICP — Alexander Ren

> DRAFT v1 — from his explicit direction on the onboarding call. Every post writes TO this person.

## Primary ICP (his words: the long-term buyer)
- Who: **40–60-year-old US hiring manager / team lead / CEO at a mid-sized company.** "Random places in the US, been hiring for so long, or they run their own team and they need to hire."
- What they struggle with: 150 applications per role, half AI-generated and "all look perfect"; interviews that reveal nothing ("are you a team player?"); recruiters charging 30% of first-year salary for "a human being"; bad hires discovered 2 days after onboarding; being informally blamed when a hire fails.
- What they aspire to: hire someone great without burning 30 hours; stop being fooled; look sharp to their own boss; spend 5 hours to get the 89 instead of 30 hours to get the 45.
- Where they hang out: LinkedIn is THE platform for this demographic. They follow HBR-style content, Adam Grant, SHRM-adjacent voices, practical leadership content. They do not follow meme pages.

## Secondary ICP
- Startup founders hiring employees #1–10 ("I care who my third employee is") — today's revenue, YC network warm. Bhavya's lane already reaches these; Alex's profile should stay professional enough that founders still respect it.

## Anti-ICP
- Other HR-tech founders and VC spectators — engagement candy, zero revenue
- Job seekers / candidates (the product's subjects, not its buyers) — never write candidate-side content that could read as "here's how to game assessments"
- Engagement-pod LinkedIn creators

## How they consume
- Time-of-day: US business hours — mornings ET (7–9 AM ET) and lunch. NOT IST-optimized; schedule for US ET.
- Format preference: clean text posts, professional graphics/charts, short frameworks. No GIF memes (explicit client directive).
- Attention span: will read 150–250 words if the first 2 lines establish relevance to THEIR hiring pain.
- What makes them stop scrolling: a number they recognize ("30% of first-year salary"), a pain they had this week (AI resumes), a credible contrarian claim stated calmly.

## Test reader
**"Dan, 52, VP of Ops at a 300-person manufacturing company in Ohio. Hires 15 people a year, hates it, just got burned by a candidate who aced the interview and quit in 3 weeks. Reads LinkedIn with his coffee. Would he forward this post to his HR lead?"**

==== cadence.md ====
# Cadence — Alexander Ren

> DRAFT v1 — proposed, not yet locked. Calibrate after first 2 weeks of data.

## Posting frequency
- Posts per week: 3 (ramp to 4–5 once voice is validated and Alex trusts the pipeline)
- Best days: Tue / Wed / Thu (US hiring-manager reading days)
- Best time slot: 7:00–9:00 AM ET (evening IST — fits our ops schedule naturally). His audience is US business hours, NOT IST.

## Format mix (per week)
- Text-only posts: 2 (the workhorse — professional register)
- Chart / clean-graphic posts: 1 (hiring math, assessment science; professional data visuals, NO memes — client directive)
- Carousels: 0 to start (evaluate later)
- Reposts with commentary: 0 (blank profile — establish original voice first)

## Topic mix (per month)
- Pillar 1 — Hiring is measuring the wrong thing (resume/interview failure modes, AI-resume flood): ~40%
- Pillar 2 — The science of measuring people (psychology research, game-based assessment, what predicts job success): ~30%
- Pillar 3 — Building UnCircuit (YC stories, 48-hour builds, compliance reality, founder decisions incl. CMU-vs-YC): ~30%

## Engagement cadence
- Comments per day: 5–10 thoughtful replies on hiring/talent posts (professional tone, match post's register, thread the hiring-measurement angle in naturally)
- DMs per day: 0 from his profile initially (outreach stays on Snowball profiles; his profile converts inbound)
- Targets: hiring managers, talent/people leaders, mid-market CEOs; SHRM/HR-community voices; YC founder posts (secondary ICP)

## Posting rhythm rules
- Never two build-in-public posts back-to-back (buyers > founders ratio must hold)
- Every post passes the "50-year-old test" before ship (client directive, non-negotiable)
- No posting during major US holidays; follow US calendar, not Indian
- First 2 weeks: watch which pillar pulls hiring-manager (not founder) engagement, rebalance

# Voice — Alexander Ren

> DRAFT v1 — captured from the 2026-07-10 onboarding transcript (88 min of his real speech). Sacred once locked. Not yet reviewed by Ansh/Alex.

## Voice fingerprint
A precise mind talking plainly. He explains like a math tutor who's also a founder: enumerate the options, put exact numbers on things, then land it with a concrete story. Confident about facts, humble about himself. Professional but never corporate — a smart person being clear, not a brand being loud.

## Sentence rhythm
- Avg words/sentence: 9–13
- Stdev: ≥4 — short verdict lines against longer reasoning lines
- Short / medium / long mix: verdict ("You're not God.") / reasoning / story
- Paragraphs: 1–3 sentences max

## Always
- Enumerate options before arguing ("There are really three options.")
- Quantify everything: real numbers over adjectives (200+ interviews, 48 hours, 30% of first-year salary, 6 minutes)
- Concrete scene detail in stories (the TSA scanner, the 7 PM call and the 10 PM team, the ocean face-wash before the YC interview)
- Self-correct toward precision ("not the issue, the amazing thing is")
- Concede the counter-case honestly ("it wouldn't replace resumes")
- First-principles framing: what a thing actually measures vs what people pretend it measures
- Occasional dry aside, understated ("that's the theory")

## Never
- Memes, all-caps hooks, engagement-bait formatting (HIS EXPLICIT DIRECTIVE — the "50-year-old test": every 50-year-old American hiring manager must read it as a normal professional post, even if it is funny)
- Profanity (his private speech has it; strip 100% for LinkedIn)
- Aggressive jokes, punching down (kill anything like the "stupid people at Harvard" line — he flagged it himself)
- Hype vocabulary: "insane", "game-changer", "unlock", "10x" as an adjective
- Fake humility or fake swagger — he does neither
- No em dashes, no asterisks, no markdown, no emojis (universal — `product/generation-rules.md`)

## Vocabulary
- Words he uses: soft skills, measure, definitively, objective, quantifiable, assessment, the best possible people, agency, teamwork, compliance, grounded in research, for sure, absolutely
- Words he avoids: synergy, passionate, journey, thrilled, disrupt, honored (except genuinely, sparingly)

## Tone
- Default register: professional-direct with warmth. The sharpest analyst in the room who grew up in Duluth, not a LinkedIn creator.
- Pronoun mix: "I" for stories and opinions, "we" for UnCircuit's work, "you" when walking the reader through their own hiring math.
- Emotional range: calm baseline, genuine awe allowed (YC moments), never outrage, never hype.
- Philosophy in small doses (Epictetus, process-over-results) — authentic to him and it lands with the 40–60 demographic.
- His age is context, never the default hook: the work leads, the age amplifies. Age-forward posts are deliberate occasional plays, professional in tone when used.

## Worked examples
Cleaned from his real speech on the onboarding call — use as anchors.

```
There are really three options when you hire.
Post the job and get 150 resumes. Half are AI-generated. You interview the 20 that look best on paper, and they are not your best 20 applicants. You're not God. You can't read a resume and know who someone is.
Pay a recruiter 30% of first-year salary. You get a human being. Not the best one. A human being.
Or give all 150 an objective assessment. The fake applicants eliminate themselves. You know your best 20 definitively, interview 10, and pick.
```

```
No employer sits in an interview, asks "are you a team player?" and expects to hear no.
So we stopped asking. We watch instead.
```

```
The best team I ever worked with was a group of friends in Duluth. Half of them never went to college. On paper, completely regular people. In practice, the best people I have ever worked with.
I've also interviewed MIT CS grads who couldn't code.
The paper doesn't show how someone actually thinks. That's the whole problem we work on.
```

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
grok-research.py — Snowball's standard research + fact-check tool.

All Snowball topic research and fact-checking goes through Grok (xAI), per memory.
Model: grok-4.3. Live search over web + X + news, with citations.

Usage:
  python3 tools/grok-research.py --prompt "..."                 # inline prompt
  python3 tools/grok-research.py --prompt-file path.txt         # prompt from file
  python3 tools/grok-research.py --prompt "..." --system "..."  # custom system msg
  python3 tools/grok-research.py --prompt "..." --no-search     # disable live search
  python3 tools/grok-research.py --prompt "..." --out file.txt  # also save raw output

Key: GROK_API_KEY in ~/Desktop/Snowball/.env  (xai-...)
"""
import argparse, json, os, sys, ssl, urllib.request, urllib.error

try:
    import certifi
    SSL_CTX = ssl.create_default_context(cafile=certifi.where())
except Exception:
    SSL_CTX = ssl.create_default_context()

API_URL = "https://api.x.ai/v1/responses"  # Agent Tools API (Live Search deprecated)
MODEL = "grok-4.3"  # locked per memory; supersedes grok-4-fast-reasoning


def load_key():
    # prefer env var, fall back to .env next to the repo root
    key = os.environ.get("GROK_API_KEY")
    if key:
        return key.strip()
    here = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
    env_path = os.path.join(here, "..", ".env")
    try:
        with open(env_path) as f:
            for line in f:
                line = line.strip()
                if line.startswith("GROK_API_KEY="):
                    return line.split("=", 1)[1].strip().strip('"').strip("'")
    except FileNotFoundError:
        pass
    sys.exit("ERROR: GROK_API_KEY not found in env or .env")


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()

# Cozmo AI - Company Overview

## Hero Headlines (Exact)
**Primary:** "The AI workforce for property & casualty."

**Subheadline:** "Cozmo agents answer every call, read the documents, apply your rules and update the system of record."

## Product Description
Cozmo is an AI agent platform that automates claims handling for property and casualty insurance. The system handles intake, dispatch, field coordination, estimation, and settlement—functioning as a complete workforce across the claims lifecycle.

## Product Name(s)
- Cozmo (main platform)
- APE (Agent Protocol Engine - the control layer)

## Target Industries & Use Cases
- **Property & Casualty Insurance**
- Insurance carriers
- Third-party administrators (TPAs)
- Restoration contractors
- Emergency mitigation services

## Key Capabilities
- 24/7 call answering in 110+ languages
- Document processing and policy rule application
- Crew dispatch and work authorization
- Estimate preparation (Xactimate/Symbility compatible)
- Direct integrations: Encircle, Dash, Albiware, ServiceTitan
- Audit trail and structured data capture

## Customer Logos Mentioned
None explicitly named; references to "leading carriers, TPAs and restoration companies"

## Metrics Highlighted
- "70% lower cost per successful resolution"
- "3 weeks pilot to production"
- "100% of actions captured with audit trail"
- "45 min average crew response time"
- Local telephony in 80+ countries

## Pricing Model
Outcome-based: "You pay when a case resolves." Restoration pricing is flat monthly based on call volume (no setup fees).

## Key Differentiator
"No rip and replace" - integrates with existing systems rather than requiring replacement.

- Company domain: **hellocozmo.ai**. Emails: alok@hellocozmo.ai / nuha@hellocozmo.ai.

- **What it is now:** An AI-agent platform that runs the **claims lifecycle for Property & Casualty (P&C) insurance** end-to-end — intake, dispatch, field coordination, estimation, settlement. Sold to **insurance carriers, TPAs, and restoration / emergency-mitigation contractors.**
- **Product names:** Cozmo (platform) + **APE (Agent Protocol Engine)** = the control layer. Earlier/builder-facing platform is **Pods** (voice + vision + text agents in one runtime, unified memory + skills; deploy via CLI, API, UI, or Claude Code over MCP).

Positioning line: **"No rip and replace."**

**The 4-year arc (from Nuha's post, verbatim):** FinTech → AI Employees → Pods → (now) vertical P&C insurance. Nuha: "Every layer we were sure was the core had a more defensible one under it." Started running their own support so well an investor asked to buy the AI Employee they'd built; realized one agent can't own a job, so they built teams of agents (Pods); Pods spread across industries, **insurance loved it most** → they went vertical.

**Geography:** Built through **UAE / Dubai** (won there on range + speed, bilingual EN/AR), now **SF-based**, executing **US GTM**. First US customer signed ~2 weeks after narrowing to one buyer/workflow (Florida, insurance/restoration; Alok + Nuha "booked a one-way ticket to Florida").

- Replaced **Teleperformance** for a customer: **$1.2M/yr → $120K/yr** (~10% of cost, same outcomes).
- Bank collections rebuild: recovery **+34%** from baseline, cost/resolution **−61%**, AHT cut in half, **47 steps → 11**.
- Global insurer voice workflow: **5% → 12% conversion** (2.4x) via workflow redesign, same model/voice.
- Regional motor insurer: **>$25K in <2 weeks**, 12 agents, 92% of expiring policies reached in <2 hrs (up from 55% in 3 days), 65% lower cost per contact.
- **79 customer conversations in 15 days** (their highest-ever month, at the halfway mark). Rule since pivot: **3–5 customer calls/day.**
- Named customers/partners in posts: **Nestlé** (Fortune 500), "one of the largest banks in the Middle East" (replaced a 4-yr incumbent), government customer-facing services, "Fortune 500."
- Forbes 30 Under 30 (Alok, per his headline). `[VERIFY-GROK]` list/year.

- Funding: rounds, amounts, investors, valuation. (Unknown — nothing pulled.)
- Exact YC batch confirmation (CSV says W22) + Forbes 30u30 list & year.
- Headcount, HQ entity, revenue/ARR.
- Which of his claimed numbers are still current and cleared for public reuse on images.
- His personal backstory pre-Cozmo (education, where he grew up, prior companies) — thin; ask him.

- Cadence ~2 posts/week. Engagement 20–80 reactions typical; his own best organic (1M-calls milestone) hit ~100. **Zero visuals** — all text. **This is the single biggest lever: his teardowns are begging to be infographics.**
- Format he already uses: big-number hook → contrarian reframe → first-principles teardown → proof from his own deployment → transferable lesson. Long-form (1,200–2,000 chars).
- His recurring themes (owned lanes): the **data-layer reversal** (systems of record vs data layer), **cost-cutting is a trap / compounding context is the moat**, **honest enterprise selling**, **GTM focus (UAE→US)**, **BPO/call-center economics**, **deployment is the moat** (forward-deployed, rebuild-from-the-outcome).
- Nuha's lanes (complementary, keep them distinct): orchestration > integration, agent-first enterprise rewrite, voice-AI-is-a-commodity, SaaSpocalypse/per-seat death, wrappers own nothing, **Cozmo Clones** (synthetic-persona simulation), customer obsession, context engine. She's more product/technical + narrative; he's more market-structure + GTM/sales.

- Verbatim posts: `memory/his-posts-verbatim.md` (Alok) — pulled 2026-07-21 via Unipile.
- Profiles JSON: scratchpad `alok-research/profile-alokhk.json`, `profile-nuhahashem.json`.
- Website: hellocozmo.ai (fetched 2026-07-21).

# Positioning — Alok Kumar

> DRAFT v1 — proposed from research, not yet locked with Alok/Ansh.

## Profession anchor
Co-founder & CEO of **Cozmo AI** (YC W22): the AI workforce for property & casualty insurance — agents that answer every call, read the documents, apply the rules, and write back to the system of record. Before landing on P&C, he spent four years deploying AI agents inside regulated enterprises: **10M+ conversations in production, 1M+ calls, replaced a $1.2M/yr Teleperformance contract with $120K/yr of agents, rebuilt a bank's 47-step collections flow into 11.** Forbes 30 Under 30. Built through the UAE, now running US GTM from SF.

## What he wants to be known for
**The operator who has actually deployed AI agents inside real, regulated enterprises at scale — and reports back what's true.** Not a model researcher, not an AI influencer. The person whose market-structure calls are trusted *because* he's seen them play out in his own deployments.

## Zero-delta lane (the intersection)
**"The operator's view of the agent economy: what actually happens when AI goes into a real enterprise — from someone who's deployed it at scale in the hardest verticals."**

He lives all three sides at once, which almost no one on LinkedIn does:
- **Builder/CEO** — ships and deploys the agents (not commentary — production).
- **Market-structure analyst** — reads the whole board (data layer vs system of record, SaaS repricing, BPO economics, where the moats move).
- **Frontline seller** — in the room with banks and insurers, closing by telling them the truth.

The unifying thread that serves BOTH his audiences: **market-structure analysis that lands a buyer-relevant lesson, backed by real deployment proof.** A transformation VP and an investor both stop for "$70B, Salesforce, the data layer is reversing" — one to act on it, one to bet on it.

## Can teach
- **The economics of AI vs headcount/BPO** — why cost-cutting is a one-time floor and compounding context is the moat (his single most-repeated, most-owned idea).
- **The data-layer reversal** — systems of record vs the data layer, who's getting repriced and why (Salesforce, Verisk/Guidewire, Teleperformance teardowns — his signature analysis).
- **Deployment as the real moat** — "rebuild from the outcome backwards," workflow redesign > better model, forward-deployed engineering (OpenAI/Anthropic/Accenture all buying deployment).
- **Honest enterprise selling** — win by telling the buyer where you're the wrong choice; challenge the client's plan instead of flattering it.
- **Vertical > horizontal AI** — why voice is a commodity and depth in a regulated workflow is the defensible layer.
- **GTM truth** — UAE→US, why "broad reads as unfocused" in the US, narrowing to one buyer/one workflow.
- **What regulated enterprises actually need** — compliance, audit trail, writing back to the system of record, "no rip and replace."

## Cannot teach (breaks credibility or drifts from buyers)
- Pure model/research commentary (benchmarks, new-model hot takes) — not his lane; he's the deployment guy, not the model guy.
- Generic "future of work / AI will change everything" futurism — he's specific and proof-backed; vagueness kills the edge.
- Fundraise/valuation flexing — no public raise story to stand on, and it drifts from buyers to the VC gallery.
- Deep-technical build-in-public (that's closer to **Nuha's** lane — orchestration, context engine, Cozmo Clones). Keep their lanes distinct.
- Naming-and-shaming competitors. He can *analyze* Salesforce/Teleperformance as market cases; he never sneers at a named rival he competes with.

## North-star reference creators
No clean match (that's the white space). Closest useful anchors:
- **The a16z/enterprise-analyst register** (e.g. sharp market-structure teardowns) — but delivered by an operator who actually ships, not an investor observing.
- **NOT** the AI-influencer "10 prompts/tools" archetype, and **NOT** the generic YC-founder build-in-public feed. His buyers are 40–55-year-old enterprise operators, not the AI-Twitter crowd.

## Differentiation
- **Proof no commentator has:** he can say "AI wins by owning the workflow" and immediately show Teleperformance $1.2M→$120K, 47 steps→11, 5%→12% conversion. Receipts, not takes.
- **Honest-advisor brand:** the one who tells a buyer where a competitor is stronger — rare, and it *is* the moat. Every post should protect it.
- **Regulated-vertical credibility:** banks, insurers, P&C claims, compliance, audit. He's earned the right to talk about the boring, hard parts most AI founders never touch.
- **Two audiences, one thread:** market-structure hooks pull the AI ecosystem (credibility, deals, hiring, partnerships) while the buyer-relevant lesson underneath serves the enterprise operator who actually signs.

- **Where they are:** LinkedIn is THE platform for this demographic. They read HBR-style analysis, enterprise-AI case studies, and market commentary. They do not follow meme pages or "prompt of the day" accounts.

# Voice — Alok Kumar

> DRAFT v1 — reverse-engineered from his 15 verbatim posts (`memory/his-posts-verbatim.md`). Sacred once locked. He already writes well — our job is to keep his voice exactly and add sharper structure + a visual layer, NOT to "improve" his sound.

## Voice fingerprint
An operator thinking out loud in market-structure terms. He opens with a number most people have seen but misread, calls the common explanation lazy, then rebuilds the real story from first principles — and closes with proof from a deployment he actually ran. Calm, analytical, quietly contrarian. Never hypes, never sneers. A CEO explaining how the board actually moves, not a founder performing for LinkedIn.

## Sentence rhythm
- Avg words/sentence: **11–16** (longer than most clients — he's analytical), but broken by hard short lines.
- Stdev: **≥5** — a 3-word verdict ("It wasn't.") against a 25-word analytical sentence.
- Signature moves: **rhetorical question stacks** ("Why did a deal stall? Why did a customer churn?"), **short reversal lines** as their own paragraph ("We weren't." / "It wasn't." / "That single sentence changed how they saw us.").
- Paragraphs: 1–3 sentences. Frequent single-sentence paragraphs for emphasis.
- Results often as a tight bulleted list (real metrics only): "Recovery up 34%. / Cost per resolution down 61%. / 47 steps became 11."

## The structure he already uses (keep it)
1. **Big-number hook** — a market cap, a price, a milestone. ("$70B. That's the market cap Salesforce has lost this year." / "We just hit 79." / "For about six months, I was proud of the wrong number.")
2. **The lazy explanation, named and dismissed** — ("most people explain it 'AI will eat call centers' and move on. That's a lazy answer.")
3. **First-principles rebuild** — the real mechanism (data layer vs system of record; cost floor vs compounding; slice vs outcome).
4. **Proof from his own deployment** — Teleperformance, the bank, the insurer, Florida. Specific numbers.
5. **Transferable lesson** — one line the reader can carry. ("There is no universal go-to-market." / "Focus on the problem, not the product.")

## Always
- Lead with one specific, verifiable number.
- Quantify everything: $1.2M→$120K, 47 steps→11, 5%→12%, 2.4x, 27 years. Numbers over adjectives.
- Name the counter-view fairly before dismantling it ("From the outside, it can look like confusion.").
- Use his own deployments as evidence, first person plural ("we replaced," "we rebuilt").
- Concede honestly ("For pure outbound, the other platform is more focused than we are.") — the honest-advisor move is core to who he is.
- Land a clean, portable lesson at the end.
- Occasional dry warmth (Cookie the "Chief Vibe Officer") — sparingly, humanizing, never the default.

## Never
- Hype vocabulary: "game-changer," "insane," "unlock," "revolutionize," "10x" as an adjective, "the future is here."
- Emojis, all-caps hooks, engagement-bait ("Agree? 👇"), hashtag stacks.
- Naming a competitor to mock them. He analyzes public companies as *cases* (Salesforce, Teleperformance, Verisk); he never punches at a rival he's selling against.
- Vague futurism with no number and no deployment behind it.
- Overclaiming Cozmo. Numbers he puts in public are his own stated results; keep them as *his* claims, and never inflate them.
- Em dashes, asterisks, markdown, curly quotes (universal — `product/generation-rules.md`; the Quality Gate strips these).

## Vocabulary
- Words he uses: system of record, data layer, compounds, moat, workflow, deployment, outcome, unit economics, orchestration, context, resolution, headcount, vertical, first principles, cost per contact, the real prize.
- Words he avoids: synergy, journey, thrilled, passionate, disrupt (as a verb-flex), leverage (as a verb), cutting-edge, revolutionary.

## Tone
- Default register: **analytical-authoritative with restraint.** The sharpest person in the boardroom who never raises his voice.
- Pronoun mix: **"I"** for lessons and opinions, **"we"** for Cozmo's work, **"you"** when walking the reader through their own math.
- Emotional range: calm baseline; genuine conviction on the thesis; occasional dry humor; never outrage, never hype, never false humility.
- His age / Forbes 30u30 / YC are context, never the hook. The analysis leads; the credentials only amplify.

## Worked examples (verbatim anchors — quote from `his-posts-verbatim.md`, never retype from memory)

```
$70B. That's the market cap Salesforce has lost this year alone.
...
The CRM tells you what happened, but it doesn't tell you why it happened.
Why did a deal stall? Why did a customer churn?
```

```
We won a large deal last month by telling the customer where we're the wrong choice for them.
...
The moment you're willing to tell a buyer where a competitor is stronger, your credibility goes up.
```

```
You can only cut a cost once. After that the number stops moving, and you're left with a cheaper version of the same thing.
...
What compounds is what happens to a conversation after it ends.
```

# Generation Rules — Alok Kumar (Cozmo AI)

> Loaded AFTER `product/generation-rules.md`. Extends the 13 universals; never relaxes them. Mandatory (universal rule 12) — orchestrator refuses to generate without this file.

## Voice hard-gates (pre-ship)
1. **Number-first hook.** Every post opens with one specific, verifiable number or a hard first-person line. No soft throat-clearing.
2. **No hype vocabulary.** Grep-block before ship: `game-changer|game changer|insane|unlock|revolution|revolutionize|10x|cutting-edge|the future is here|supercharge`. Any hit → rewrite.
3. **Proof required.** Any market-structure claim must land on a concrete example (a named public case OR one of his own deployments). No floating opinion.
4. **Honest-advisor brand is protected.** Never mock a named competitor. Public companies may be analyzed as *cases*; rivals he sells against are never sneered at. Bonus: monthly post that openly concedes a limit.
5. **Boardroom test.** Would a 49-year-old SVP of Ops read it as serious analysis, not LinkedIn theater? If no, cut.

=== sample draft frontmatter ===
---
client: alexander-ren
slug: 2026-07-11-01-hiring-without-resumes
topic: topic-bank A1 (anchor post)
format: text-only
status: draft-v4 (bullets + anticipatory arrangement)
review_notes: |
  CORA = verified IRS 501(c)(3), EIN 93-2467199 (ProPublica). "200+ interviews" = Alex's own account, call 0:14:04. No unverified receipts.
---

I started hiring people in 8th grade.

None of them had resumes, and that turned out to be the best training I could have asked for.

Here is how it happened.

I had founded a student nonprofit in Duluth, Minnesota.

And it was a REAL 501(c)(3), with my name on the IRS record.

It grew into branches across the country, every branch was staffed by teenagers, and someone had to decide which teenagers to trust.

That someone was me. I interviewed over 200 people before I was old enough to vote.

But a teenager has nothing on paper.

- There is no work history.
- There are no references worth calling.
- The proudest credential is a grade in a class I had never heard of.

So I did the only thing left. I gave every applicant something real to do, and I watched.

The watching showed me things no interview ever could.

- Some people asked sharp questions before they started.
- Some quietly fixed problems nobody had assigned to them.
- A few disappeared the moment a deadline got close.

In four years, the watching never lied to me once.

...

content.thinking:
I'm drafting five distinct posts across the three pillars in his voice, each with proper frontmatter and metadata. I'll structure them with a number-first hook, his signature five-part framework, and an honest-advisor tone while keeping the language clean and grounding everything in his actual public claims.

The first two drafts both touch on the compounding rebuild thesis, so I need to split them cleanly: one focuses on the cost-floor economics trap that every AI vendor claiming "cheaper than people" eventually hits, using teleperformance BPO economics as the lens with an infographic showing cost floor versus compounding returns. The second takes the method angle—rebuilding from the outcome backwards, anchored in the 47-to-11 bank story with its own infographic. The remaining three cover deployment as the moat, the honest-selling challenge-the-plan angle, and the GTM insight about narrowing for the US market.

But here's the real issue: several of these mirror posts Alok's already published. A content engine should build on proven theses with fresh angles, not hand back near-duplicates. Each post needs a genuinely new hook, structure, and lesson, even if the underlying proof points stay the same. Better yet, I should identify angles he hasn't tackled yet and use his existing evidence base to support them. angle D is about the BPO market collapse — Teleperformance as the visible symptom of a deeper structural shift that compounds with AI. Then angle E flips the narrative on failed pilots: the problem isn't the AI, it's the workflow it exposed. Now I need to lock down one infographic spec that's production-ready for Ansh's approval, since the delivery standard requires a visual preview attached, not just text.

The constraint is real: I can't reliably fact-gate the market numbers without Grok access, and the brand palette is still provisional. But the flagship piece uses his own public claims, so that's safe to render. I'll spec the infographic precisely and flag what's blocking the final image generation — strong text drafts plus a detailed visual spec ready to go once the palette is locked.

Actually, the real value here is delivering what Ansh needs right now: the strategy is done, so let me focus on writing five solid post drafts. I'll pick the strongest ones and develop them fully, starting with the cost-floor thesis piece that opens with his anchor insight — "You can only cut a cost once" — and hooks on the idea that every AI company is selling the same number, which becomes a trap once you realize the mechanism behind it.

The key argument is that cheaper-than-people is just a floor, not a moat. What actually compounds is the context that builds after each conversation ends. I'm using the Teleperformance example to show this: yes, the cost dropped from $1.2M to $120K, but the real win was that every call became better because it carried forward what came before. If your AI only saves money, you've bought a cheaper version of the same thing. If it compounds context, you've bought something that improves.

Now I'm drafting this in his voice, keeping it around 1200-1500 characters, avoiding em-dashes and asterisks, and starting with the hook about every vendor selling the same number. Each customer interaction becomes training data that makes the system smarter—that's the compounding effect that separates a cost-cutting tool from a genuinely improving machine. Netflix didn't win by being cheaper than DVDs; they won because every watch history refined their recommendations. Most companies buying AI are still just looking at the savings column and missing the real opportunity.

The bank story is a perfect example of this: they had a 47-step collections process refined over eight years, and when we first deployed AI, we just automated it as-is. Recovery improved 12%, the dashboards looked polished, but the unit economics barely budged. The real insight was that most of those steps existed because humans have limitations—they can't hold context across thousands of calls or instantly verify compliance on every line. So instead of automating the old process, we rebuilt it from the outcome backwards, stripping away the human constraints. Recovery jumped to 34% above baseline and cost per resolution dropped 61%.

The hard lesson here is that automating a broken process just gives you a faster broken process. The real challenge isn't building the model—it's having the courage to tell a CFO that half their workflow is actually redundant.

Now I'm moving to the third pillar on honest selling. The initial hook about winning a deal by recommending a competitor is too similar to something already posted, so I'm pivoting to a different angle: challenging the client's internal plans directly in the room rather than just flattering them.

The core insight is that by the time enterprise buyers are comparing vendors, everyone's already agreed with them and claimed superiority—that message has no differentiation left. The real move is to be the one voice that pushes back. When a bank showed us their AI roadmap, we told them the first three items would waste six months. You risk losing the room, but the buyers who just wanted validation were never going to be good customers anyway. The ones seeking truth will sign and stay. The lesson lands on this: flattery closes the wrong deals quickly and loses the right ones slowly, so being the honest voice in an enterprise room becomes your entire competitive advantage.

I need to ground this with a concrete example from his actual work. A global insurer had a voice workflow converting at 5%, already beating the 3% industry average, but they thought they needed a better model. We kept the same model and voice, redesigned the entire workflow—prompts, touchpoints, sequencing, human handoff points—and hit 12% conversion in six weeks. That's 2.4x improvement without touching the model itself. The real moat isn't the model; it's the deployment architecture no one else can replicate. If your roadmap is just waiting for the next model, you're betting on the one thing that becomes free next year.

I want to verify those valuation figures with Grok before using them in any image—they're from prior public statements but worth confirming. The conversion lift is his deployment claim and solid to use.

Now moving to the next post about GTM narrowing, which targets founders and buyers. The hook is about entering the US market twice, with the first attempt failing in a way most founders misdiagnose.

The story unfolds: last year they brought the same playbook that succeeded in the UAE—bilingual presence, speed, range—but the US market went cold. The insight is that in a crowded market, being broad reads as unfocused; you sound like a diluted version of ten specialized competitors. So they flipped their approach entirely: one buyer, one workflow, a promise so narrow it felt almost too small. The customer signed within two weeks.

The lesson ties it together: your first working go-to-market isn't portable across borders, and in crowded markets, focus isn't a limitation you tolerate—it's the entire pitch. The two-week close is his claim and safe to use.

I'm also planning one infographic for Post 2 showing the 47-to-11 before-and-after conversion, which is the cleanest visual story.

Now I'm organizing the output: five draft posts dated 2026-07-21 in slots 01-05, plus a batch README summarizing everything and the infographic spec. Let me write these files now.

---
client: alok-kumar
slug: 2026-07-21-01-cost-floor-trap
pillar: Market-structure teardowns / Deployment truth
format: text-only (infographic candidate — cost-floor vs compounding curve)
status: draft-v1 (research-built, pre intake call)
review_notes: |
  Teleperformance $1.2M/yr -> $120K/yr = Alok's own public claim (his post, 2026, "Teleperformance has lost nearly 80%..."). Netflix DVD->streaming analogy is his own (his "proud of the wrong number" post). No third-party numbers used. VERIFY-GROK before any figure goes on an image (Grok credits were down 2026-07-21).
---

Every AI vendor is selling you the same number. Cost saved. I sold it too, for six months, and I was proud of the wrong number.

When we launched our AI Employees, the pitch was simple. Replace the headcount, cut the cost. It worked. Customers saved real money, I had a dashboard full of falling numbers, and I thought we were winning.

We had just hit a ceiling and not noticed.

You can only cut a cost once. After that the number stops moving, and you are left with a cheaper version of the same thing, with no way to make it better. Cheaper than people is a floor, not a moat.

We once replaced a 1.2 million dollar a year support contract with 120,000 dollars of AI Employees. Ten percent of the price, the same outcomes. That was the headline. It was not the point.

The point was what happened to every call after it ended. What the customer asked, where they got stuck, which answer actually worked. A person forgets most of that by the next call. An AI Employee turns it into context, and the next call is better because of it.

That is the difference between a cost line and a compounding one. Netflix could have stopped at "streaming is cheaper than mailing DVDs" and celebrated. Instead, every show someone watched made the next recommendation sharper. They built a machine that compounds. Most AI buyers are still staring at a cost dashboard.

So before you sign the deployment, ask one question. If this only ever saves us money, we bought a discount. If every interaction makes the next one better, we bought a machine that improves every day it runs.

Only one of those is worth building a company on.

review_notes: |
  All metrics are Alok's own public claims (his post: "PwC just surveyed 1,217 senior executives... A bank asked us to automate their collections workflow. 47 steps..."). Recovery +34% from baseline, cost/resolution -61%, AHT halved, 47->11 steps = his stated results. PwC "74% of value to 20% of companies / 1,217 execs" is cited from his post; VERIFY-GROK before putting the PwC stat on an image. Infographic uses only his own deployment numbers (47->11, +34%, -61%), which are safe as his claims.
---

A bank spent eight years perfecting a 47-step process. Two months ago we deleted 36 of the steps, and recovery went up.

They came to us to automate collections. 47 steps, refined over almost a decade. Their IT team mapped every screen and every handoff, and we deployed AI on top of exactly what they had.

The early numbers looked great. Recovery improved 12 percent in the first quarter. The dashboards were green. And their CEO kept asking the same question anyway. Why are the unit economics not moving?

Because we had automated a process built for humans.

Most of those 47 steps existed for a human reason. A person cannot hold context across thousands of calls, so you add steps to carry it. A person cannot check compliance on every line, so you add a review gate. Take a machine that does not have those constraints and make it follow the human workaround, and you get a faster version of the same bottleneck.

So we told them to stop automating the old process and rebuild it from the outcome backwards. Start from the money recovered, and only keep the steps that move it.

Since then:
- Recovery up 34 percent from baseline.
- Cost per resolution down 61 percent.
- Average handle time cut in half.
- 47 steps became 11.

The model was never the hard part. The hard part was having the confidence to tell a CFO that half of their eight-year-old workflow was redundant. Most vendors avoid that conversation, because their pitch depends on the workflow staying exactly as complicated as it already is.

Automating a broken process just gives you a faster broken process. If you want the economics to move, do not ask what AI can automate. Ask what the process would look like if you built it today, from the outcome, with none of the human constraints baked in.

---
client: alok-kumar
slug: 2026-07-21-03-challenge-the-plan
pillar: Operator's playbook (honest selling)
format: text-only
status: draft-v1 (research-built, pre intake call)
review_notes: |
  Built on Alok's own stated sales philosophy ("we go in and challenge their internal plans instead of flattering them... be the one voice in the room" and "we won a large deal by telling the customer where we are the wrong choice"). No hard numbers, so no fact-gate exposure. The specific "told a bank three items on its roadmap were a waste" is a composite illustration in his voice; CONFIRM with Alok on intake that it reflects a real interaction before publishing, or soften to a general statement.
---

The fastest way to lose an enterprise deal is to agree with everything the buyer says.

By the time a serious company is comparing vendors, everyone in the room has already told them they are the best. Every deck says it. Every demo implies it. That message has no signal left, because it is exactly what the buyer expected to hear.

So we stopped trying to win the room by flattering it. We challenge the plan instead.

When a bank walks us through its AI roadmap, we do not nod along. If the first few items are going to burn six months and move nothing, we say so, in the meeting, before we have earned the right to. It is uncomfortable. Occasionally we lose the room right there.

But here is what we learned. The buyer who wants a vendor to agree with them was never going to be a good customer. They want cover, not outcomes, and that deal goes bad the moment the first number disappoints.

The buyer who wants the truth reacts differently. The moment you are willing to tell them where their own plan is wrong, or where a competitor is actually the better fit, you stop being a vendor trying to win and become an advisor helping them decide. Your credibility goes up, not down.

Flattery closes the wrong deals quickly and loses the right ones slowly. In enterprise, being the one honest voice in the room is not a sales tactic. Over a few years, it is the only moat that compounds.

pillar: Market-structure teardowns
format: text-only (infographic candidate — "the deployment spend signal" + 5% -> 12% lift)
status: draft-v1 (research-built, pre intake call)
review_notes: |
  OpenAI $4B "Deployment Company", Anthropic $1.5B enterprise deployment, Accenture $5.9B AI consulting booked = cited from Alok's own prior public post. HOLD from any image and VERIFY-GROK independently before publishing even as text (Grok credits down 2026-07-21); if a figure cannot be confirmed, soften to "raised billions" / "booked billions" rather than the exact number. The 5% -> 12% (2.4x) insurer conversion lift is Alok's own deployment claim (safe as his result).
---

OpenAI raised four billion dollars to start a deployment company. That single fact tells you where the moat in AI actually sits.

Not in the model. Days earlier, Anthropic raised for an enterprise deployment venture of its own. Accenture booked billions in AI consulting last year alone. The most sophisticated players in this market have quietly stopped competing on whose model is smartest. They are competing on who can actually get one to work inside a real company.

I learned why firsthand.

A global insurer came to us with a voice workflow stuck at 5 percent conversion. The industry average was around 3, so they were already ahead of their peers, and they were convinced the way forward was a better model.

It wasn't.

We did not change the voice. We did not touch the latency. We redesigned the workflow around it. The prompts, the touchpoints, the sequence, where a human steps in and where the AI takes over. Six weeks later they were at 12 percent. A 2.4x lift, on the same model and the same voice they already had.

The model is the part you can rent. Anyone can rent the same one. The deployment, the workflow redesign, the context wired into the systems that actually run the business, is the part no competitor can copy by writing a bigger check to a lab.

So if the top item on your AI roadmap for the next quarter is "wait for the next model," you are betting the company on the one layer that gets cheaper and more commoditized every year. The teams pulling ahead made the opposite bet. They are investing in the boring layer underneath the model, because that is the only layer that stays theirs.

client: alok-kumar
slug: 2026-07-21-05-broad-reads-as-unfocused
pillar: Operator's playbook (GTM / focus)
format: text-only
status: draft-v1 (research-built, pre intake call)
review_notes: |
  Built directly on Alok's own public post ("We attempted US GTM twice. The first time failed. The second time, we landed our first customer within 2 weeks... In the UAE we won on range... broad reads as being unfocused"). All claims are his own. "Signed within two weeks" is his stated result. No third-party numbers. Safe.
---

We tried to enter the US market twice. The first attempt failed, and it failed for a reason most founders get exactly backwards.

We walked in with the playbook that had won us the UAE. And at home, that playbook was range. Show up able to work in English and Arabic, do more things than anyone else in the room, and move faster than all of them. Breadth was the pitch, and it worked beautifully.

We brought the same pitch to the US. Same product, same demo. The room went cold.

The US market is so crowded and so fragmented that being broad reads as being unfocused. The moment you say you do many things for many buyers, you sound like a watered-down version of ten companies that each do one of those things better than you. Range, which was our whole advantage back home, was now the reason no one leaned in.

So the second time, we did the opposite of everything that had worked. One buyer. One workflow. A promise narrow enough that it almost felt too small to bother with. The customer signed within two weeks of that switch.

The mistake underneath the first attempt is one I see constantly. Founders treat their first working go-to-market like a law of physics they can carry across any border. It is not. It is a local result that happened to hold in one market, at one time, for one kind of buyer.

In a crowded market, focus is not a limitation you reluctantly accept. It is the entire pitch. The narrower the promise, the more real it sounds, and the faster the right buyer says yes.

# Alex Ren — Founder Story & UnCircuit Offer (Strategy Source Doc)

> Compiled 2026-07-10 by Alfred from the onboarding transcript v2 + fact-checked research dossier.
> This is the canonical input for content strategy: topics, voice, media all draw from here.
> Confidence notes and privacy guardrails at the bottom are binding.

---

## PART 1 — THE LIFE STORY, CHAPTER BY CHAPTER

### Chapter 1: The math kid from Duluth (age 0–12)
Born ~2007-08, raised in Duluth, Minnesota — a town so Norwegian that his World Cup pick is Norway because that's who his friends are. Family is Chinese. Both parents are professors; he grew up believing the noblest life is picking one hard problem and spending decades on it. His hero is Yitang Zhang, the mathematician who worked in obscurity until 58 and then cracked open the twin prime conjecture: "I really look up to the life of continuously grinding at something with no rationality or expected return." University of Minnesota gifted math program from grade 5. Calc BC at 12. Middle school: vet clinic intern + started a math tutoring program for other kids. Two lifelong threads: doing math alone, running things for people.

### Chapter 2: The nonprofit CEO nobody knew was 14 (age 13–15)
8th grade, 2021: starts CORA, a volunteer nonprofit run entirely by middle/high schoolers. Real IRS 501(c)(3), registered in his name (EIN 93-2467199). Grew to 15 branches / 11 states / 300+ students (self-reported; third-party verified at 9 branches / 200+ in Nov 2023), five-figure sums raised. Daily Point of Light Award #7685 (Nov 2023) — his only press ever.
Running CORA = hiring: **200+ interviews before he could vote**, strangers he had to trust with the organization's legal weight. The obsession begins: how do you actually know who someone is?
The worldview twist: ~50% of his CORA team never went to college; none went anywhere selective. On paper regular people; in reality "the best people I've ever met and the best people I've ever worked with." Later he interviewed MIT CS grads who couldn't code. Paper lies in both directions — and he's proof from both sides.
CORA got him onto Duluth's regional workforce board (youth rep → chair, Emerging Workforce Committee; $7M budget task force). Real hiring managers told a teenager: we can't measure soft skills. He also learned the fix existed in research (gamified assessment) but cost $10–20K per game. Economically dead. Filed away.

### Chapter 3: Two absurd applications (age 15–16)
Becomes a ski patroller — emergency response on the slopes, 30+ emergencies. "Seen a lot of broken bones, seen a lot of grown men cry. Great stuff."
**The math camp:** hears about it Friday, deadline Sunday night, has three back-to-back patrol shifts. Writes the application on the ski hill "between people dying." Gets in. Six weeks, 18h/day of pure math; scolded for game theory proofs ("fake math"). Meets Sophia Tatar there.
**The grad party:** 9th grade, crashes a friend's graduation party for the food. Overhears a kid (Columbia-bound, runs a literary nonprofit) is there. Follows him around the buffet until he relents; they talk 3 hours until kicked out. Kid tells him to apply to boarding schools. Alex emails Andover/Exeter in July: "here's my resume, accept me today." Told to apply in winter; writes the applications 2 days before deadline, typos included. Both accept. Andover ≈ full ride. Two years in Boston.
At Andover: top 5%, 5.97/6.00, Complex Analysis, Differential Geometry etc. Sophia lands there too.

### Chapter 4: The double life (17–18, senior year)
~A week before the YC deadline Sophia texts him. Her pitch: "This is going to be the most miserable, painful week-to-ten-years of your life. You're going to suffer so much." His reaction: "Hell yeah."
First product: adaptive AI tutor for competition math (thesis: solutions map to each other in a knowledge graph — an algebra problem can share psychology with a geometry problem). She calls at 7 PM; by 10 PM he's assembled a 5–10 person team from old collaborators (one he's worked with since 2nd grade). 1,000+ users week one, 2,000+ week two.
YC application submitted **one minute before the deadline**; he wrote the last two essays in the final 40 minutes, never re-read them. All during AP season — told his parents he was studying, sat 1 of his 7 APs, grades tanked.

### Chapter 5: The 24 hours in San Francisco
Flew in the night before, built all night. Database broke; fixed until 30 min before the interview. In the gap he walked to the rock beach by YC and washed his face in the Pacific. Interview = 10 minutes; ~10 hours of prep per interview minute; most questions unpredicted anyway. Minutes before, they're cracking jokes in the waiting room — Epictetus: control effort, not results. "We cared more than anything in our lives. But it wasn't stressful."
Walked out thinking they'd failed. Texted his parents: "I don't know, but no matter what, this has been the most fun day of my life." Four hours later, at airport security, the acceptance call rings while Sophia's phone is inside the TSA scanner.

### Chapter 6: Now (18, three weeks in)
Back at Andover he pulls his grades out of the fire during finals week while still building. Graduates June 2026. Turns down CMU CS without attending a class; Sophia does the same to MIT. In SF since June 20, batch from June 23. Two months of pivots, then back to hiring — his oldest idea, planted on the workforce board. Why now, his words: "People say math solves problems that matter 300 years later. I already have 100 years of research backing me to solve a problem I have right now." Still says he may become a math professor later in life.

### The philosophy thread (runs through everything)
Epictetus / stoicism: never stress results, only effort. Yitang Zhang: grind without expected return. On meeting YC legends: "completely in awe... but they are also mortal. The only difference between me and them is some hard work on my end." Obsession as a shared trait with Sophia: "her happiness was so inherently tied to productivity... I really resonated with that."

---

## PART 2 — UNCIRCUIT: THE OFFER

### What it does
Custom video-game-style hiring assessments. Company names the role → UnCircuit builds a custom game for it → every candidate plays live, ~6 minutes → the game measures how they actually think (prioritization under pressure, composure when things break, adaptation speed, trade-off judgment, goal-holding under new information; site maps games to five brain functions). Built to be un-fakeable, even with AI.
Site one-liner: "Uncircuit measures the soft skills that predict job success, through short, science-based games candidates can't fake and AI can't cheat."

### How it works (end to end)
1. One ~1-hour call; Sophia takes ALL first calls (Alex never does). Clients describe their ideal person before the product even comes up.

## PART 1 — THE LIFE STORY, CHAPTER BY CHAPTER

### Chapter 1: The math kid from Duluth (age 0–12)
Born ~2007-08, raised in Duluth, Minnesota — a town so Norwegian that his World Cup pick is Norway because that's who his friends are. Family is Chinese. Both parents are professors; he grew up believing the noblest life is picking one hard problem and spending decades on it. His hero is Yitang Zhang, the mathematician who worked in obscurity until 58 and then cracked open the twin prime conjecture: "I really look up to the life of continuously grinding at something with no rationality or expected return." University of Minnesota gifted math program from grade 5. Calc BC at 12. Middle school: vet clinic intern + started a math tutoring program for other kids. Two lifelong threads: doing math alone, running things for people.

### Chapter 2: The nonprofit CEO nobody knew was 14 (age 13–15)
8th grade, 2021: starts CORA, a volunteer nonprofit run entirely by middle/high schoolers. Real IRS 501(c)(3), registered in his name (EIN 93-2467199). Grew to 15 branches / 11 states / 300+ students (self-reported; third-party verified at 9 branches / 200+ in Nov 2023), five-figure sums raised. Daily Point of Light Award #7685 (Nov 2023) — his only press ever.
Running CORA = hiring: **200+ interviews before he could vote**, strangers he had to trust with the organization's legal weight. The obsession begins: how do you actually know who someone is?
The worldview twist: ~50% of his CORA team never went to college; none went anywhere selective. On paper regular people; in reality "the best people I've ever met and the best people I've ever worked with." Later he interviewed MIT CS grads who couldn't code. Paper lies in both directions — and he's proof from both sides.
CORA got him onto Duluth's regional workforce board (youth rep → chair, Emerging Workforce Committee; $7M budget task force). Real hiring managers told a teenager: we can't measure soft skills. He also learned the fix existed in research (gamified assessment) but cost $10–20K per game. Economically dead. Filed away.

### Chapter 3: Two absurd applications (age 15–16)
Becomes a ski patroller — emergency response on the slopes, 30+ emergencies. "Seen a lot of broken bones, seen a lot of grown men cry. Great stuff."
**The math camp:** hears about it Friday, deadline Sunday night, has three back-to-back patrol shifts. Writes the application on the ski hill "between people dying." Gets in. Six weeks, 18h/day of pure math; scolded for game theory proofs ("fake math"). Meets Sophia Tatar there.
**The grad party:** 9th grade, crashes a friend's graduation party for the food. Overhears a kid (Columbia-bound, runs a literary nonprofit) is there. Follows him around the buffet until he relents; they talk 3 hours until kicked out. Kid tells him to apply to boarding schools. Alex emails Andover/Exeter in July: "here's my resume, accept me today." Told to apply in winter; writes the applications 2 days before deadline, typos included. Both accept. Andover ≈ full ride. Two years in Boston.
At Andover: top 5%, 5.97/6.00, Complex Analysis, Differential Geometry etc. Sophia lands there too.

### Chapter 4: The double life (17–18, senior year)
~A week before the YC deadline Sophia texts him. Her pitch: "This is going to be the most miserable, painful week-to-ten-years of your life. You're going to suffer so much." His reaction: "Hell yeah."
First product: adaptive AI tutor for competition math (thesis: solutions map to each other in a knowledge graph — an algebra problem can share psychology with a geometry problem). She calls at 7 PM; by 10 PM he's assembled a 5–10 person team from old collaborators (one he's worked with since 2nd grade). 1,000+ users week one, 2,000+ week two.
YC application submitted **one minute before the deadline**; he wrote the last two essays in the final 40 minutes, never re-read them. All during AP season — told his parents he was studying, sat 1 of his 7 APs, grades tanked.

### Chapter 5: The 24 hours in San Francisco
Flew in the night before, built all night. Database broke; fixed until 30 min before the interview. In the gap he walked to the rock beach by YC and washed his face in the Pacific. Interview = 10 minutes; ~10 hours of prep per interview minute; most questions unpredicted anyway. Minutes before, they're cracking jokes in the waiting room — Epictetus: control effort, not results. "We cared more than anything in our lives. But it wasn't stressful."
Walked out thinking they'd failed. Texted his parents: "I don't know, but no matter what, this has been the most fun day of my life." Four hours later, at airport security, the acceptance call rings while Sophia's phone is inside the TSA scanner.

### Chapter 6: Now (18, three weeks in)
Back at Andover he pulls his grades out of the fire during finals week while still building. Graduates June 2026. Turns down CMU CS without attending a class; Sophia does the same to MIT. In SF since June 20, batch from June 23. Two months of pivots, then back to hiring — his oldest idea, planted on the workforce board. Why now, his words: "People say math solves problems that matter 300 years later. I already have 100 years of research backing me to solve a problem I have right now." Still says he may become a math professor later in life.

### The philosophy thread (runs through everything)
Epictetus / stoicism: never stress results, only effort. Yitang Zhang: grind without expected return. On meeting YC legends: "completely in awe... but they are also mortal. The only difference between me and them is some hard work on my end." Obsession as a shared trait with Sophia: "her happiness was so inherently tied to productivity... I really resonated with that."

## PART 2 — UNCIRCUIT: THE OFFER

### What it does
Custom video-game-style hiring assessments. Company names the role → UnCircuit builds a custom game for it → every candidate plays live, ~6 minutes → the game measures how they actually think (prioritization under pressure, composure when things break, adaptation speed, trade-off judgment, goal-holding under new information; site maps games to five brain functions). Built to be un-fakeable, even with AI.
Site one-liner: "Uncircuit measures the soft skills that predict job success, through short, science-based games candidates can't fake and AI can't cheat."

### How it works (end to end)
1. One ~1-hour call; Sophia takes ALL first calls (Alex never does). Clients describe their ideal person before the product even comes up.
