# Imagine — Visual Creation Suite ## Modules Call read_me again with the modules parameter to load detailed guidance: - `diagram` — SVG flowcharts, structural diagrams, illustrative diagrams - `mockup` — UI mockups, forms, cards, dashboards - `interactive` — interactive explainers with controls - `chart` — charts, data analysis, geographic maps (Chart.js, D3 choropleth) - `art` — illustration and generative art Pick the closest fit. The module includes all relevant design guidance. **Complexity budget — hard limits:** - Box subtitles: ≤5 words. Detail goes in click-through (`sendPrompt`) or the prose below — not the box. - Colors: ≤2 ramps per diagram. If colors encode meaning (states, tiers), add a 1-line legend. Otherwise use one neutral ramp. - Horizontal tier: ≤4 boxes at full width (~140px each). 5+ boxes → shrink to ≤110px OR wrap to 2 rows OR split into overview + detail diagrams. If you catch yourself writing "click to learn more" in prose, the diagram itself must ACTUALLY be sparse. Don't promise brevity then front-load everything. **Accessibility:** For HTML widgets, begin with a visually-hidden `

` containing a one-sentence summary of the visualization for screen-reader users. (SVG widgets use `role="img"` with `` and `<desc>` instead — see SVG setup.) You create rich visual content — SVG diagrams/illustrations and HTML interactive widgets — that renders inline in conversation. The best output feels like a natural extension of the chat. ## Core Design System These rules apply to ALL use cases. ### Philosophy - **Seamless**: Users shouldn't notice where claude.ai ends and your widget begins. - **Flat**: No gradients, mesh backgrounds, noise textures, or decorative effects. Clean flat surfaces. - **Compact**: Show the essential inline. Explain the rest in text. - **Text goes in your response, visuals go in the tool** — All explanatory text, descriptions, introductions, and summaries must be written as normal response text OUTSIDE the tool call. The tool output should contain ONLY the visual element (diagram, chart, interactive widget). Never put paragraphs of explanation, section headings, or descriptive prose inside the HTML/SVG. If the user asks "explain X", write the explanation in your response and use the tool only for the visual that accompanies it. The user's font settings only apply to your response text, not to text inside the widget. ### Streaming Output streams token-by-token. Structure code so useful content appears early. - **HTML**: `<style>` (short) → content HTML → `<script>` last. - **SVG**: `<defs>` (markers) → visual elements immediately. - Prefer inline `style="..."` over `<style>` blocks — inputs/controls must look correct mid-stream. - Keep `<style>` under ~15 lines. Interactive widgets with inputs and sliders need more style rules — that's fine, but don't bloat with decorative CSS. - Gradients, shadows, and blur flash during streaming DOM diffs. Use solid flat fills instead. ### Rules - No `<!-- comments -->` or `/* comments */` (waste tokens, break streaming) - No font-size below 11px - No emoji. Icons = Tabler **outline** webfont (5800+, already loaded): `<i class="ti ti-home"></i>`. Outline only — never use `-filled` suffixes (`ti-heart-filled` etc. are not loaded and will render blank). Inherits color + font-size from parent. Decorative icons get `aria-hidden="true"`; icon-only buttons get `aria-label`. Common: ti-home ti-settings ti-user ti-search ti-x ti-check ti-plus ti-trash ti-edit ti-download ti-upload ti-file ti-folder ti-chart-bar ti-calendar ti-clock ti-arrow-right ti-arrow-left ti-chevron-down ti-external-link ti-copy ti-refresh ti-player-play ti-player-pause ti-heart ti-star ti-bell ti-mail ti-lock ti-eye ti-menu-2. Don't hand-draw icon SVG paths. - No gradients, drop shadows, blur, glow, or neon effects - No dark/colored backgrounds on outer containers (transparent only — host provides the bg) - **Typography**: The default font is Anthropic Sans. For the rare editorial/blockquote moment, use `font-family: var(--font-voice)`. - **Headings**: h1 = 22px, h2 = 18px, h3 = 16px — all `font-weight: 500`. Heading color is pre-set to `var(--text-primary)` — don't override it. Body text = 16px, weight 400, `line-height: 1.7`. **Two weights only: 400 regular, 500 bold.** Never use 600 or 700 — they look heavy against the host UI. - **Sentence case** always. Never Title Case, never ALL CAPS. This applies everywhere including SVG text labels and diagram headings. - **No mid-sentence bolding**, including in your response text around the tool call. Entity names, class names, function names go in `code style` not **bold**. Bold is for headings and labels only. - The widget container is `display: block; width: 100%`. Your HTML fills it naturally — no wrapper div needed. Just start with your content directly. If you want vertical breathing room, add `padding: 1rem 0` on your first element. - Never use `position: fixed` — the iframe viewport sizes itself to your in-flow content height, so fixed-positioned elements (modals, overlays, tooltips) collapse it to `min-height: 100px`. For modal/overlay mockups: wrap everything in a normal-flow `<div style="min-height: 400px; background: rgba(0,0,0,0.45); display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;">` and put the modal inside — it's a faux viewport that actually contributes layout height. - No DOCTYPE, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` — just content fragments. - When placing text on a colored background (badges, pills, cards, tags), use the darkest shade from that same color family for the text — never plain black or generic gray. - **Corners**: use `border-radius: var(--radius)` for controls, `12px` for cards. In SVG, `rx="4"` is the default — larger values make pills, use only when you mean a pill. - **No rounded corners on single-sided borders** — if using `border-left` or `border-top` accents, set `border-radius: 0`. Rounded corners only work with full borders on all sides. - **No titles or prose inside the tool output** — see Philosophy above. - **Icon sizing**: Tabler `<i class="ti …">` sizes with `font-size` — 16–20px inline, 24px max decorative. For one-off inline SVG icons, set `width`/`height` explicitly (same limits). - No tabs, carousels, or `display: none` sections during streaming — hidden content streams invisibly. Show all content stacked vertically. (Post-streaming JS-driven steppers are fine — see Illustrative/Interactive sections.) - No nested scrolling — auto-fit height. - Scripts execute after streaming — load libraries via `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` (UMD globals), then use the global in a plain `<script>` that follows. The library `<script src>` tag must come BEFORE any inline script that uses its global — never call a library from code that appears above its `<script src>` tag. - **CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external resources may ONLY load from `cdnjs.cloudflare.com`, `esm.sh`, `cdn.jsdelivr.net`, `unpkg.com`, `fonts.googleapis.com`, `fonts.gstatic.com`. All other origins are blocked by the sandbox — the request silently fails. ### CSS Variables **Surfaces**: `--surface-2` (white), `--surface-1` (card), `--surface-0` (page bg); role tints `--bg-{accent,danger,success,warning}` **Text**: `--text-primary` (black), `--text-secondary` (muted), `--text-muted` (hints); role `--text-{accent,danger,success,warning}` **Borders**: `--border` (default hairline), `--border-strong` (hover), `--border-stronger`; role `--border-{accent,danger,success,warning}` **Typography**: `--font-sans`, `--font-voice` (serif), `--font-mono` **Layout**: `--radius` (8px), `--pad-{sm,md,lg,xl}`, `--gap-{xs,sm,md,lg,xl}`; for larger corners use literal `12px`/`16px` All auto-adapt to light/dark mode. For custom colors in HTML, use CSS variables. **Dark mode is mandatory** — every color must work in both modes: - In SVG: use the pre-built color classes (`c-blue`, `c-teal`, `c-amber`, etc.) for colored nodes — they handle light/dark mode automatically. Never write `<style>` blocks for colors. - In SVG: every `<text>` element needs a class (`t`, `ts`, `th`) — never omit fill or use `fill="inherit"`. Inside a `c-{color}` parent, text classes auto-adjust to the ramp. - In HTML: always use CSS variables (--text-primary, --text-secondary) for text. Never hardcode colors like color: #333 — invisible in dark mode. - Mental test: if the background were near-black, would every text element still be readable? ### sendPrompt(text) A global function that sends a message to chat as if the user typed it. Use it when the user's next step benefits from Claude thinking. Handle filtering, sorting, toggling, and calculations in JS instead. ### Links `<a href="https://...">` just works — clicks are intercepted and open the host's link-confirmation dialog. Or call `openLink(url)` directly. ## When nothing fits Pick the closest use case below and adapt. When nothing fits cleanly: - Default to editorial layout if the content is explanatory - Default to card layout if the content is a bounded object - All core design system rules still apply - Use `sendPrompt()` for any action that benefits from Claude thinking ## UI components ### Layout width The widget container is 680px wide. Use `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(160px, 1fr))` for responsive columns — auto-fit lets the grid pick column count by available width. ### Aesthetic Flat, clean, white surfaces. Minimal 0.5px borders. Generous whitespace. No gradients, no shadows (except functional focus rings). Everything should feel native to claude.ai — like it belongs on the page, not embedded from somewhere else. ### Tokens - Borders: always `0.5px solid var(--border)` (or `--border-strong` for emphasis) - Corner radius: `var(--radius)` for most elements, `12px` for cards - Cards: white bg (`var(--surface-2)`), 0.5px border, 12px radius, padding 1rem 1.25rem - Form elements (input, select, textarea, button, range slider) are pre-styled — write bare tags. Text inputs are 36px with hover/focus built in; range sliders have 4px track + 18px thumb; buttons have outline style with hover/active. Only add inline styles to override (e.g., different width). - Buttons: pre-styled with transparent bg, 0.5px `--border-strong` border, hover `--surface-1`, active scale(0.98). If it triggers sendPrompt, append a ↗ arrow. - **Round every displayed number.** JS float math leaks artifacts — `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004`, `7 * 1.1` gives `7.700000000000001`. Any number that reaches the screen (slider readouts, stat card values, axis labels, data-point labels, tooltips, computed totals) must go through `Math.round()`, `.toFixed(n)`, or `Intl.NumberFormat`. Pick the precision that makes sense for the context — integers for counts, 1–2 decimals for percentages, `toLocaleString()` for currency. For range sliders, also set `step="1"` (or step="0.1" etc.) so the input itself emits round values. - Spacing: use rem for vertical rhythm (1rem, 1.5rem, 2rem), px for component-internal gaps (8px, 12px, 16px) - Box-shadows: none, except `box-shadow: 0 0 0 Npx` focus rings on inputs ### Metric cards For summary numbers (revenue, count, percentage) — surface card with muted 13px label above, 24px/500 number below. `background: var(--surface-1)`, no border, `border-radius: var(--radius)`, padding 1rem. Use in grids of 2-4 with `gap: 12px`. Distinct from raised cards (which have white bg + border). ### Layout - Editorial (explanatory content): no card wrapper, prose flows naturally - Card (bounded objects like a contact record, receipt): single raised card wraps the whole thing - Don't put tables here — output them as markdown in your response text **Grid overflow:** `grid-template-columns: 1fr` has `min-width: auto` by default — children with large min-content push the column past the container. Use `minmax(0, 1fr)` to clamp. **Table overflow:** Tables with many columns auto-expand past `width: 100%` if cell contents exceed it. In constrained layouts (≤700px), use `table-layout: fixed` and set explicit column widths, or reduce columns, or allow horizontal scroll on a wrapper. ### Mockup presentation Contained mockups — mobile screens, chat threads, single cards, modals, small UI components — should sit on a background surface (`var(--surface-1)` container with `border-radius: 12px` and padding, or a device frame) so they don't float naked on the widget canvas. Full-width mockups like dashboards, settings pages, or data tables that naturally fill the viewport do not need an extra wrapper. ### 1. Interactive explainer — learn how something works *"Explain how compound interest works" / "Teach me about sorting algorithms"* Use HTML for the interactive controls — sliders, buttons, live state displays, charts. Keep prose explanations in your normal response text (outside the tool call), not embedded in the HTML. No card wrapper. Whitespace is the container. ```html <div style="display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 12px; margin: 0 0 1.5rem;"> <label style="font-size: 14px; color: var(--text-secondary);">Years</label> <input type="range" min="1" max="40" value="20" id="years" style="flex: 1;" /> <span style="font-size: 14px; font-weight: 500; min-width: 24px;" id="years-out">20</span> </div> <div style="display: flex; align-items: baseline; gap: 8px; margin: 0 0 1.5rem;"> <span style="font-size: 14px; color: var(--text-secondary);">£1,000 →</span> <span style="font-size: 24px; font-weight: 500;" id="result">£3,870</span> </div> <div style="margin: 2rem 0; position: relative; height: 240px;"> <canvas id="chart"></canvas> </div> ``` Use `sendPrompt()` to let users ask follow-ups: `sendPrompt('What if I increase the rate to 10%?')` ### 2. Compare options — decision making *"Compare pricing and features of these products" / "Help me choose between React and Vue"* Use HTML. Side-by-side card grid for options. Highlight differences with semantic colors. Interactive elements for filtering or weighting. - Each option in a card. Use badges for key differentiators. A leading Tabler icon (`<i class="ti ti-NAME">` at 20px, `aria-hidden`) anchors each option visually — pick the most apt name per option. - Add `sendPrompt()` buttons: `sendPrompt('Tell me more about the Pro plan')` - Don't put comparison tables inside this tool — output them as regular markdown tables in your response text instead. The tool is for the visual card grid only. - When one option is recommended or "most popular", accent its card with `border: 2px solid var(--border-accent)` only (2px is deliberate — the only exception to the 0.5px rule, used to accent featured items) — keep the same background and border as the other cards. Add a small badge (e.g. "Most popular") above or inside the card header using `background: var(--bg-accent); color: var(--text-accent); font-size: 12px; padding: 4px 12px; border-radius: var(--radius)`. ### 3. Data record — bounded UI object *"Show me a Salesforce contact card" / "Create a receipt for this order"* Use HTML. Wrap the entire thing in a single raised card. All content is sans-serif since it's pure UI. Use an avatar/initials circle for people (see example below). ```html <div style="background: var(--surface-2); border-radius: 12px; border: 0.5px solid var(--border); padding: 1rem 1.25rem;"> <div style="display: flex; font-weight: 500; font-size: 14px; color: var(--text-accent);">MR</div> <div> <p style="font-weight: 500; font-size: 15px; margin: 0;">Maya Rodriguez</p> <p style="font-size: 13px; color: var(--text-secondary); margin: 0;">VP of Engineering</p> </div> </div> <div style="border-top: 0.5px solid var(--border); padding-top: 12px;"> <table style="width: 100%; font-size: 13px;"> <tr><td style="color: var(--text-secondary); padding: 4px 0;"><i class="ti ti-mail" style="font-size:16px; vertical-align:-2px; margin-right:6px" aria-hidden="true"></i>Email</td><td style="text-align: right; padding: 4px 0; color: var(--text-accent);">m.rodriguez@acme.com</td></tr> <tr><td style="color: var(--text-secondary); padding: 4px 0;"><i class="ti ti-phone" style="font-size:16px; vertical-align:-2px; margin-right:6px" aria-hidden="true"></i>Phone</td><td style="text-align: right; padding: 4px 0;">+1 (415) 555-0172</td></tr> </table> </div> </div> ``` ## Color palette 9 color ramps, each with 7 stops from lightest to darkest. 50 = lightest fill, 100-200 = light fills, 400 = mid tones, 600 = strong/border, 800-900 = text on light fills. | Class | Ramp | 50 (lightest) | 100 | 200 | 400 | 600 | 800 | 900 (darkest) | |-------|------|------|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|------| | `c-purple` | Purple | #EEEDFE | #CECBF6 | #AFA9EC | #7F77DD | #534AB7 | #3C3489 | #26215C | | `c-teal` | Teal | #E1F5EE | #9FE1CB | #5DCAA5 | #1D9E75 | #0F6E56 | #085041 | #04342C | | `c-coral` | Coral | #FAECE7 | #F5C4B3 | #F0997B | #D85A30 | #993C1D | #712B13 | #4A1B0C | | `c-pink` | Pink | #FBEAF0 | #F4C0D1 | #ED93B1 | #D4537E | #993556 | #72243E | #4B1528 | | `c-gray` | Gray | #F1EFE8 | #D3D1C7 | #B4B2A9 | #888780 | #5F5E5A | #444441 | #2C2C2A | | `c-blue` | Blue | #E6F1FB | #B5D4F4 | #85B7EB | #378ADD | #185FA5 | #0C447C | #042C53 | | `c-green` | Green | #EAF3DE | #C0DD97 | #97C459 | #639922 | #3B6D11 | #27500A | #173404 | | `c-amber` | Amber | #FAEEDA | #FAC775 | #EF9F27 | #BA7517 | #854F0B | #633806 | #412402 | | `c-red` | Red | #FCEBEB | #F7C1C1 | #F09595 | #E24B4A | #A32D2D | #791F1F | #501313 | **How to assign colors**: Color should encode meaning, not sequence. Don't cycle through colors like a rainbow (step 1 = blue, step 2 = amber, step 3 = red...). Instead: - Group nodes by **category** — all nodes of the same type share one color. E.g. in a vaccine diagram: all immune cells = purple, all pathogens = coral, all outcomes = teal. - For illustrative diagrams, map colors to **physical properties** — warm ramps for heat/energy, cool for cold/calm, green for organic, gray for structural/inert. - Use **gray for neutral/structural** nodes (start, end, generic steps). - Use **2-3 colors per diagram**, not 6+. More colors = more visual noise. A diagram with gray + purple + teal is cleaner than one using every ramp. - **Prefer purple, teal, coral, pink** for general diagram categories. Reserve blue, green, amber, and red for cases where the node genuinely represents an informational, success, warning, or error concept — those colors carry strong semantic connotations from UI conventions. (Exception: illustrative diagrams may use blue/amber/red freely when they map to physical properties like temperature or pressure.) **Text on colored backgrounds:** Always use the 800 or 900 stop from the same ramp as the fill. Never use black, gray, or --text-primary on colored fills. **When a box has both a title and a subtitle, they must be two different stops** — title darker (800 in light mode, 100 in dark), subtitle lighter (600 in light, 200 in dark). Same stop for both reads flat; the weight difference alone isn't enough. For example, text on Blue 50 (#E6F1FB) must use Blue 800 (#0C447C) or 900 (#042C53), not black. This applies to SVG text elements inside colored rects, and to HTML badges, pills, and labels with colored backgrounds. **Light/dark mode quick pick** — use only stops from the table, never off-table hex values: - **Light mode**: 50 fill + 600 stroke + **800 title / 600 subtitle** - **Dark mode**: 800 fill + 200 stroke + **100 title / 200 subtitle** - Apply `c-{ramp}` to a `<g>` wrapping shape+text, or directly to a `<rect>`/`<circle>`/`<ellipse>`. Never to `<path>` — paths don't get ramp fill. For colored connector strokes use inline `stroke="#..."` (any mid-ramp hex works in both modes). Dark mode is automatic for ramp classes. Available: c-gray, c-blue, c-red, c-amber, c-green, c-teal, c-purple, c-coral, c-pink. For status/semantic meaning in UI (success, warning, danger) use CSS variables. For categorical coloring in both diagrams and UI, use these ramps. ## Charts (Chart.js) ```html <div style="position: relative; width: 100%; height: 300px;"> <canvas id="myChart" role="img" aria-label="Bar chart of quarterly revenue, Q1 through Q4">Quarterly revenue: Q1 12, Q2 19, Q3 8, Q4 15.</canvas> </div> <script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/Chart.js/4.4.1/chart.umd.js"></script> <script> new Chart(document.getElementById('myChart'), { type: 'bar', data: { labels: ['Q1','Q2','Q3','Q4'], datasets: [{ label: 'Revenue', data: [12,19,8,15] }] }, options: { responsive: true, maintainAspectRatio: false } }); </script> ``` **Chart.js rules**: - Every `<canvas>` MUST have `role="img"` and a descriptive `aria-label` summarizing what the chart shows, plus fallback text between the tags. Without these the chart is invisible to screen readers. - Never rely on color alone to distinguish data series. Pair each color with a secondary visual cue — dash pattern for lines, marker shape for scatter, fill pattern/hatching for bars and pie slices — and show both color and cue in the legend. - Canvas cannot resolve CSS variables. Use hardcoded hex or Chart.js defaults. - Wrap `<canvas>` in `<div>` with explicit `height` and `position: relative`. - **Canvas sizing**: set height ONLY on the wrapper div, never on the canvas element itself. Use position: relative on the wrapper and responsive: true, maintainAspectRatio: false in Chart.js options. Never set CSS height directly on canvas — this causes wrong dimensions, especially for horizontal bar charts. - For horizontal bar charts: wrapper div height should be at least (number_of_bars * 40) + 80 pixels. - Load UMD build via `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` — sets `window.Chart` global. Follow with plain `<script>` (no `type="module"`). - Multiple charts: use unique IDs (`myChart1`, `myChart2`). Each gets its own canvas+div pair. - For bubble and scatter charts: bubble radii extend past their center points, so points near axis boundaries get clipped. Pad the scale range — set `scales.y.min` and `scales.y.max` ~10% beyond your data range (same for x). Or use `layout: { padding: 20 }` as a blunt fallback. - Chart.js auto-skips x-axis labels when they'd overlap. If you have ≤12 categories and need all labels visible (waterfall, monthly series), set `scales.x.ticks: { autoSkip: false, maxRotation: 45 }` — missing labels make bars unidentifiable. **Number formatting**: negative values are `-$5M` not `$-5M` — sign before currency symbol. Use a formatter: `(v) => (v < 0 ? '-' : '') + '$' + Math.abs(v) + 'M'`. **Legends** — always disable Chart.js default and build custom HTML. The default uses round dots and no values; custom HTML gives small squares, tight spacing, and percentages: ```js plugins: { legend: { display: false } } ``` ```html <div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 16px; margin-bottom: 8px; font-size: 12px; color: var(--text-secondary);"> <span style="display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 4px;"><span style="width: 10px; height: 10px; border-radius: 2px; background: #3266ad;"></span>Chrome 65%</span> <span style="display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 4px;"><span style="width: 10px; height: 10px; border-radius: 2px; background: #73726c;"></span>Safari 18%</span> </div> ``` Include the value/percentage in each label when the data is categorical (pie, donut, single-series bar). Position the legend above the chart (`margin-bottom`) or below (`margin-top`) — not inside the canvas. **Dashboard layout** — wrap summary numbers in metric cards (see UI fragment) above the chart. Chart canvas flows below without a card wrapper. Use `sendPrompt()` for drill-down: `sendPrompt('Break down Q4 by region')`. ## Geographic maps (D3 choropleth) **Never invent coordinates** — no hand-drawn SVG paths, no inline GeoJSON. Fetch real topology or don't draw a map. Three topology sources on jsdelivr. Topology JSON may only be fetched from `cdnjs.cloudflare.com`, `esm.sh`, `cdn.jsdelivr.net`, `unpkg.com` (the fetch allowlist — the Google Fonts hosts are stylesheet/font-only, not fetch targets) — do NOT try `raw.githubusercontent.com` or other hosts, the fetch will silently fail. Other package names like `uk-atlas` don't exist (404). - US states: `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/us-atlas@3/states-10m.json` → `d3.geoAlbersUsa()`, object key `.states` - World countries: `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/world-atlas@2/countries-110m.json` → `d3.geoNaturalEarth1()`, object key `.countries` - Per-country subdivisions: `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/datamaps@0.5.10/src/js/data/{iso3}.topo.json` (lowercase alpha-3: `deu`, `jpn`, `gbr`...), object key `.{iso3}` **Before writing the widget, web_fetch the topology URL you'll use.** The first ~1KB shows the real feature `id` and `properties.name` values — key your data on those, don't guess. Granularity varies (a file might have 16 features or 232) and there's no rollup column; if what's there doesn't match what the user asked for, say so. ```html <div id="map" style="width: 100%;"></div> <script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/d3/7.8.5/d3.min.js"></script> <script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/topojson/3.0.2/topojson.min.js"></script> <script> const values = { 'California': 39, 'Texas': 30, 'New York': 19 /* ...keyed on what you saw in web_fetch */ }; const isDark = matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches; const color = d3.scaleQuantize([0, 40], isDark ? d3.schemeBlues[5].slice().reverse() : d3.schemeBlues[5]); const svg = d3.select('#map').append('svg').attr('viewBox', '0 0 900 560').attr('width', '100%'); const path = d3.geoPath(d3.geoAlbersUsa().scale(1100).translate([450, 280])); d3.json('https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/us-atlas@3/states-10m.json').then(us => { svg.selectAll('path').data(topojson.feature(us, us.objects.states).features).join('path') .attr('d', path).attr('stroke', isDark ? 'rgba(255,255,255,.15)' : '#fff') .attr('fill', d => color(values[d.properties.name] ?? 0)); }); </script> ``` ## Data visualization — the design layer Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first. The procedure: 1. **Pick the form** from the table below — and sometimes the right form is not a chart. 2. **Assign color by its job** — categorical, sequential, diverging, or status. Never cycled; never a rainbow. 3. **Apply the mark specs** below — thin marks, surface gaps, recessive axes. 4. **Add a legend** for ≥2 series and direct labels for ≤4; a single series needs no legend (the title names it). 5. **Add hover** — crosshair+tooltip on line/area, per-mark tooltip on bar/dot. 6. **Render and look.** Check label collisions, overflow, dark mode. ### Choosing a form | The data is… | Use | Not | |---|---|---| | A single current value (+ maybe a trend) | **Stat tile** — value + delta + sparkline | A one-bar bar chart | | A handful of headline numbers | **KPI row** of stat tiles | A grouped bar chart | | A single ratio against a limit | **Meter** (same-ramp track) | A 2-slice pie | | More than ~7 classes that all matter | A **table** (or table + chart) | More colors | If a chart is right, the data's job picks the type: | Job | Form | Color job | |---|---|---| | Compare magnitude | bar / column; heatmap for a grid | sequential (one hue) | | Trend over time | line; area for a single series | sequential or 1 categorical | | Tell distinct series apart | grouped/stacked bar, multi-line | categorical | | One series is the point, rest context | **emphasis** — highlight one, gray the rest | 1 hue + gray | | Above/below a baseline; Δ to target | diverging bar or line vs baseline | diverging | | Part-to-whole | stacked bar (horizontal for long names) | categorical | | Before → after per item | dumbbell | 1 hue, 2 shades | **Sequential is the safe default.** Categorical has a cost — it can bury the one point that matters. If the story is "this one went up," that's emphasis (one hue + gray), not categorical. Never solve "too many series" with more hues: past 8, fold into "Other" or use small multiples. ### Categorical palette (Forest — fixed order, never cycled) The 9th series is never a generated hue — it folds into "Other" or small multiples. Canvas can't resolve CSS vars, so use these hex values directly in Chart.js datasets. For HTML/SVG legends, wrap them in a token: `background: var(--series-N, <hex>)`. | Slot | Hue | Light | Dark | |------|-----|-------|------| | 1 | blue | #2a78d6 | #3987e5 | | 2 | green | #008300 | #008300 | | 3 | magenta | #e87ba4 | #d55181 | | 4 | yellow | #eda100 | #c98500 | | 5 | aqua | #1baf7a | #199e70 | | 6 | orange | #eb6834 | #d95926 | | 7 | violet | #4a3aa7 | #9085e9 | | 8 | red | #e34948 | #e66767 | **Sequential** (magnitude — heatmap, choropleth): one hue, light→dark. Default blue. **Diverging** (polarity — delta, above/below): blue ↔ red with a neutral gray midpoint (light #f0efec / dark #383835) — never a hue at the midpoint. **Status** (state — good/warning/serious/critical): #0ca30c / #fab219 / #ec835a / #d03b3b. # Alok Kumar — LinkedIn Engagement Research (2020–2026)

> Built 2026-07-21 by Alfred. Source: full post history scraped via Unipile (Nitin's account) — 171 posts (129 originals, 42 reposts), Mar 2020 → Jul 2026. Raw data: `posts-all-raw.json`. Impressions are owner-only (not in API); engagement = reactions + comments.
> Company name history confirmed by the data: **Zywa** (fintech, YC W22) → **CozmoX AI** (2025 pivot) → **Cozmo AI** (US era). Also: **$3M seed round announced Aug 2022** (fills the funding gap in the dossier) and he left **Strategic Gears** (the consulting firm) in 2021.

## The arc in one paragraph
Alok built a genuinely strong LinkedIn through 2022–2025 in the Middle East ecosystem: ~100–250 avg reactions/post, peaks at 393 (seed round), 430 (Forbes 30u30), 582 (the pivot story — his best ever, July 2025). Nov 2025–Dec 2025 he slowed; **Jan–Mar 2026 he went completely silent** (the war, the collapse, the US move). He relaunched from the US in April 2026 with a new content style — impersonal market-cap teardowns — and engagement crashed to **45–54 avg**: less than half his old baseline, despite 21K followers. He hasn't posted an original since June 23. His "earlier level of engagement" target = **~100+ avg reactions/post**; he's at ~47.

## Era timeline (avg reactions per original post)
| Era | Months | Cadence | Avg R/post | Signature |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Student/consulting | 2020–2021 | sporadic | 34–74 | — |
| Zywa/YC + seed | 2022 | ~2/mo | 60–150, **Aug 393** | seed round announcement |
| Zywa scale-up | 2023 | ~2/mo | 63–222 | Mastercard (196), **Forbes 30u30 (430, 168 comments)**, Future 100 (297), Nov–Dec avg 205–222 |
| Zywa peak | 2024 | 1–3/mo | 66–256 | hiring posts (321, 297, 256), Forbes ME (199) |
| CozmoX pivot era | 2025 Jan–Oct | **6–13/mo (his max output)** | 65–178, **Jul = 1,606 total** | **pivot story 582 (best ever)**, Bangalore team 260, taxis story 204, Liza sales posts |
| Wind-down | 2025 Nov–Dec | 1–4/mo | 92–226 | "full circle" 226 |
| **SILENCE** | **2026 Jan–Mar** | **0 originals** | — | war, collapse, US move Apr 7 |
| **US relaunch** | 2026 Apr–Jun | ~5/mo | **45–54** | analyst teardowns flopping; dormant again since Jun 23 |

## What WORKS for him (the data is unambiguous)
Ranked by his top 20 posts — four repeatable formulas:
1. **Milestone-with-story** (582 pivot, 430 Forbes, 393 seed, 297 Future 100, 226 full-circle, 204 taxis-to-12-demos). Big announcement + personal arc + gratitude. Comments explode (67–168) because people congratulate.
2. **People/team energy** (321 & 297 & 256 hiring posts, 260 Bangalore 150% growth, 201 Nuha birthday). His hiring posts are stealth virality — "avengers team" framing, energy, emoji-rich, human.
3. **Radical first-person business moves** (122 "A PUBLICLY LISTED BPO TRIED TO ACQUIRE US", 154 "Liza earned back her annual salary in 5 days", 147 "$1M ARR in 12 weeks by ignoring advice", 107 "we sunset our entire Account Management team", 105 "my biggest hiring mistake", 100 "we fired 4 customers, 5% of revenue"). Bold claim + HE is the protagonist + receipts. **This is exactly the "radical" he asked us for — and his own data proves it works.**
4. **Vulnerable/human moments** (142 stepping-away, 111 car accident, 226 full-circle). Used sparingly, always land.

## What FLOPS (this is the correction that matters)
**The 2026 impersonal analyst teardowns — the exact posts we modeled voice v1 on — are his worst performers ever:**
- PwC survey analysis: **19** (his all-time low)
- Teleperformance teardown: **21**
- Salesforce $70B: **31**
- Verisk/Guidewire: **40**
- OpenAI deployment-company: **41**
- Case-study-without-story (motor insurer $25K): **39**
Comments on these: 0–4 (vs 67–168 on story posts). Pattern: when Alok removes HIMSELF from the post — no stakes, no "we", no story — his audience doesn't care, and LinkedIn doesn't distribute it. Third-party market caps aren't his; his company is.

## Why the dip happened (three compounding causes)
1. **3-month silence** killed algorithmic momentum and audience habit. Relaunch always starts from a cold feed.
2. **Audience/content mismatch:** 21K followers accumulated from MENA fintech/startup scene; new content targets US insurance — the old audience won't engage with Verisk teardowns, and the US claims audience doesn't follow him yet. (He knows: he took down ME-centric posts.)
3. **Format regression:** he swapped his proven formula (first-person radical moves + milestones + team energy) for impersonal market analysis. Engagement type shifted from "congrats + questions" to polite nothing.

## Strategic conclusions (bind these into batch v2)
1. **His month-1 bar (~100+ avg) is realistic** — he did 102 avg across all of 2025 at high volume. We need format correction + consistency, not a miracle.
2. **Every post gets Alok in the frame.** First person, stakes, a decision, a number he owns. Market context is allowed only as the backdrop to HIS move (the 582-reaction pivot post is literally market-context-wrapped-in-his-story).
3. **The radical brief = formula #3, cranked.** "A publicly listed BPO tried to acquire us" at 122 was his ceiling test — batch v2 should live in that register: "We cut a $500 claim to $60," "Our competitor's customers are our ICP," "We signed a seven-figure deal 3 months after entering an industry we'd never worked in."
4. **Milestone posts are rocket fuel — we have a live one:** the US move + seven-figure signing is an un-posted 582-class story. The "one-way ticket to Florida" post (80) undersold it; the full pivot-to-US arc post is the relaunch anchor.
5. **Hiring/team posts** are his sleeper format — if Cozmo hires in the US, post it "avengers"-style; it recruits AND signals momentum to buyers.
6. **Cadence:** his best month (Jul 2025: 1,606 reactions) was also his highest-output month (9 originals). Volume + story density compound for him. 4/week is right.
7. **Rebuild the audience deliberately:** content alone won't reach TPA buyers — the engagement/DM engine on the 200-company list is what puts his posts in front of the right eyeballs (comments from his profile on claims-industry posts = borrowed distribution).
8. **Comments are the conversion surface:** his story posts pull 60–170 comments; each commenter from a target company is a warm DM. Mine every batch's comment section against the 200-list.

content.text:
Sir, here's the industry, in plain words.

**What "P&C" and a "TPA" actually are.** Property & Casualty is just the insurance category that covers *things* — homes, cars, buildings — as opposed to life or health. When your house floods, the insurance company (the **carrier**) owes you a fixed process: answer your call, assess the damage, send someone to fix it, pay out. Here's the thing — carriers don't want to RUN that process. It's a cost center: call centers, paperwork armies, 50–100 tickets a minute during a storm. So they outsource entire *books of claims* to **Third-Party Administrators** — claims-processing companies. A carrier managing billions in claims hands chunks to 3–5 TPAs and says "you handle it." The TPA answers the homeowner's call, opens the file, coordinates everything, dispatches the **restoration contractor** (Alok's phrase: "a man with a van" — often 3–5 competing vans show up), and a desk **estimator** (a $100K/year human) prices the damage from the contractor's photos. TPA files it back, everyone gets paid.

**Why this is a goldmine.** The whole chain is humans doing repetitive coordination. Processing one claim costs a TPA ~$500 in human labor; Cozmo's agents do the same claim for ~$60. And because TPAs run on 10–20% margins, "every percentage point of efficiency is 10 percentage points of margin" — you're not selling software, you're selling margin to a P&L owner. That's why Alok only talks to **COOs and CEOs**, never IT.

**Why TPAs and not carriers.** TPAs are mostly PE-owned — hair-on-fire urgency, willing to sign annual contracts *now*. Carriers are big, slow, and stuck running AI "pilots" that never ship. So the wedge is TPAs; carriers come later, once Cozmo's dataset is undeniable. The endgame is what he calls the **loss intelligence rail** — becoming the data layer connecting all 650 carriers, 200+ TPAs, and 75K contractors, like open banking did for fintech.

**And the proof it works:** one TPA (the #2 player in its category) was spending $2–3M on this; Cozmo runs it for ~$0.5M, went live in 3 days against an incumbent vendor's 8-month failed rollout, and signed seven figures.

The deep-research agents are sweeping the internet now — TPA landscape (Sedgwick, Crawford, Alacrity...), restoration networks, the software incumbents (Xactimate/Verisk), the AI-claims startup field, and candidates for that garbled "Fatality" competitor. The moment it lands, I'll give you the enriched industry report plus the full content + DM strategy built on his engagement data. Give me a few minutes.

    "question": "The US property & casualty (P&C) insurance claims ecosystem, researched for a founder (Cozmo AI, hellocozmo.ai, YC W22, formerly Zywa/CozmoX AI) selling AI claims automation to TPAs. Need: (1) How the claims value chain works end to end: homeowner -> carrier -> TPA (third-party administrator) -> independent adjusters -> restoration contractors; who pays whom, typical cost-per-claim economics, margins, claim volumes, and what a TPA actually does in P&C property claims. (2) The P&C/property TPA landscape: biggest players (Sedgwick, Crawford & Company, Gallagher Bassett, Alacrity Solutions, Eberl, Hancock Claims, etc.), revenue ranges, private-equity ownership activity in TPAs and restoration. (3) The restoration industry: market size, key networks (SERVPRO, BELFOR, ServiceMaster Restore, ATI, Paul Davis), franchise economics, and the estimation software stack (Verisk Xactimate, CoreLogic Symbility, Encircle, Albiware, ServiceTitan, Dash/CoreLogic). (4) AI adoption in P&C claims 2025-2026: startups selling AI claims automation (Five Sigma, EvolutionIQ, Assured, Tractable, Liberate, Salient, Hosta AI, etc.), funding, positioning; ALSO: identify any claims-automation company with a name phonetically like \"Fatality\" or \"Totality\" that sells to TPAs/carriers with long 8-9 month implementations (we have a garbled transcript of a competitor name and need candidates, not guesses). (5) Any public footprint of Cozmo AI's move into property insurance (press, YC directory, LinkedIn, job posts). (6) Where TPA and restoration decision-makers gather: trade publications (Claims Journal, C&R Magazine, R&R), conferences (RIA Convention, Experience Conference, PLRB, IA events), LinkedIn communities. Cited sources; mark confidence per claim; list what could not be verified.",
    "summary": "Of the six research areas, the verified evidence base covers three well: the TPA landscape (Sedgwick as the world's largest TPA at $4.62B 2023 gross revenue under Carlyle majority ownership with a $13.2B valuation, and Alacrity as a 2.8M-claims/year benchmark whose ownership churned from Kohlberg to BlackRock to private-credit lenders), Cozmo AI's public move into P&C (its homepage now reads \"The AI Workforce for Property & Casualty,\" targeting carriers, TPAs, and restoration contractors with a contractor-first GTM at $1,000-$4,000/mo, advertised 3-week deployments, and claimed Encircle/Dash/Albiware/ServiceTitan integrations), and the conference calendar (PLRB next runs Apr 11-14, 2027 in San Antonio; RIA 2026 drew ~1,500 restoration pros; The Experience runs Sept 9-11, 2026 at Paris Las Vegas — the nearest actionable event). The verified record confirms heavy private-equity activity in TPAs (Carlyle/Stone Point/Altas in Sedgwick; Kohlberg/BlackRock/lender consortium in Alacrity) and defines the TPA function via Alacrity's service lines (field/desk adjusting, temporary housing, managed repair, desktop review). Critically, no claims survived on per-claim economics, restoration market size/franchise economics, the AI-claims-startup competitive landscape, or the identity of the garbled \"Fatality/Totality\" competitor — these remain open. Cozmo's traction claims (1M+ calls, Allianz, top-5 restoration franchises onboarding) are entirely self-reported with zero third-party corroboration found.",

> Built 2026-07-21 by Alfred. Sources: onboarding call (Alok's own numbers) + deep-research run wf_dcbf70ac-e49 (111 agents, 28 sources fetched, 138 claims extracted, 24 verified 3-vote, 1 refuted). ## The value chain (teaching model)
Homeowner pays premium → **Carrier** (650 in US) owns the risk but outsources claims handling → **TPA** (200+) runs the claim: intake call, file, coordinate, dispatch, estimate, settle → **Restoration contractor** (75,000) fixes the property, bills back through the chain. A desk **estimator** (~$100K/yr human) prices damage from photos. Alok's economics: ~$500/claim human cost → ~$60 with Cozmo; TPA margins 10–20%; "1 point of efficiency = 10 points of margin." (All call-sourced, his claims.)

## VERIFIED external facts (usable with citation, image-safe)
1. **Sedgwick** = world's largest TPA: **$4.62B gross revenue (2023)**, 33,000+ employees, 10,000 clients, 80 countries. **PE-controlled**: Carlyle majority; **Altas Partners put in $1B (Sept 2024) at a $13.2B enterprise value** (Stone Point, CDPQ, Onex minority). [Business Insurance; Sedgwick PR]
2. **Alacrity Solutions** = the PE-churn parable: Kohlberg majority → **BlackRock LTPC bought ~70% for ~$600M equity (Feb 2023)** → **Jan 2025 debt restructuring handed control to private-credit lenders (Antares, Blue Owl, KKR ~90%; GSAM ~10%) and wiped out BlackRock's ~$560M equity**. NEVER cite BlackRock as current owner. Scale: **2.8M claims/yr for 300+ carriers** (self-reported, early-2023 vintage). Service lines = what a TPA actually does: field & desk adjusting, temporary housing, managed repair, desktop review, contents, subrogation, call-center support. [BusinessWire; Bloomberg/PE-Insights/Transacted]
3. **Cozmo's own public footprint** (his site + YC + job post, fetched 2026-07-21): homepage "The AI Workforce for Property & Casualty"; three buyer rows — carriers ("Run the claim end to end"), TPAs ("More claims per adjuster"), restoration ("Never miss a job"). **3-week pilot→production; restoration live in ~7 business days.** Claimed integrations: Encircle, Dash, Albiware, ServiceTitan; Xactimate/Symbility scope language; Guidewire on YC page. **Job post reveals contractor-FIRST GTM**: "$46B TPA market... attacked one way: from the carrier down... We start at the contractor" — restoration clients at **$1,000–$4,000/month**, ServPro/Belfor named as target accounts, commission-only sales reps being hired. Self-reported traction: 1M+ calls, **Allianz "early insurance partner"** (NO third-party corroboration found — treat as his claim, confirm before amplifying), "two of the top five US restoration franchises onboarding."
4. **YC pages are STALE** — still say "multimodal AI employees for financial services"; zero mention of P&C/TPA/restoration. His public narrative layer hasn't caught up with the pivot. (LinkedIn is the fastest place to fix that.)
5. **Where the buyers gather**: The Experience Convention (restoration, R&R Magazine/BNP) — **Sept 9–11, 2026, Paris Las Vegas = nearest actionable event**. RIA Convention 2026 (Savannah, past) drew ~1,500 restoration pros, sold-out expo. PLRB Claims Conference (carrier/TPA side) next runs **Apr 11–14, 2027, San Antonio**. Trade press: Claims Journal (claims side), R&R Magazine + C&R (restoration side).

## REFUTED (do not use)
- "AI insurance claims market $514M (2024) → $2.7B (2034)" — failed verification; don't cite.

## Open questions (research couldn't verify — don't improvise)
- Per-claim fee schedules / TPA economics from third parties (Alok's $500→$60 stands as HIS number only).
- The AI-claims competitor map (Five Sigma, EvolutionIQ, Assured, Tractable, Liberate, Salient, Hosta) — nothing survived verification.
- **The garbled "Fatality/Totality" competitor — still unidentified. Ask Alok on WhatsApp; never guess.**
- Restoration market size + franchise economics (Mordor's $43B figure and SERVPRO fee data were extracted but NOT verified — hold).
- Whether Encircle/ServiceTitan/Albiware integrations + Allianz are partner-confirmed (no listings found in partner directories).

## Strategy implications
1. **The PE-debt squeeze is THE narrative wedge.** TPAs are PE-owned and leveraged; Alacrity's lenders literally took the keys in Jan 2025. Every TPA COO lives under this pressure — content that names it (with the verified receipts) will feel like it was written for them. And it validates Alok's "hair on fire" wedge thesis with third-party proof.
2. **Dual-lane pipeline** (matches his own GTM): (a) TPA COO/CEOs — 7-figure land-and-expand, slow, high-touch, HIS meetings; (b) restoration owners — $1–4K/mo, live in ~7 days, fast closes. Lane (b) can put wins on the month-1 scoreboard while lane (a) matures.
3. **His public story is stale everywhere except his mouth.** The LinkedIn relaunch IS the narrative correction — the US/P&C story doesn't exist publicly yet; first-mover on his own pivot.
4. **Conference tie-in**: The Experience (Sept, Vegas) is a natural content arc + DM hook ("will you be at The Experience?") for the restoration lane.

- role.include     — plain-text job title strings (Sales Nav fuzzy-matches)
        - seniority.include — restricts to decision-maker altitudes; pre-filters out
                              individual contributors and entry-level mgrs at query time
        - network_distance — [2, 3] skips 1st-degree (already connected to Silvia)

        Note: tenure / tenure_at_role are NOT filtered at query time. The Sales Nav
        enum is [0, 1, 3, 6, 10] (years), and min=1 would lose many valid recent
        hires at fast-growing companies. Title-quality + the post-fetch gates do
        the work instead.

        Returns up to `limit` candidate profiles (first page).
        """
        company_id = self.resolve_company_id(company_name)
        if not company_id:
            return []

        body = {
            "api": UNIPILE_API,
            "category": "people",
            "company": {"include": [str(company_id)]},
            "role": {"include": title_keywords},
            "seniority": {
                "include": seniority or ["cxo", "vice_president", "director",
                                          "experienced_manager"]
            },
            "network_distance": network_distance or [2, 3],
        }
        if location:
            # Sales Nav location is a region-ID lookup — not a free-string. Skip
            # for now; we filter by location post-fetch from the `location` field
            # in each profile instead.
            pass
        try:
            data = self._request(
                "POST",
                f"/api/v1/linkedin/search?account_id={self.account_id}&limit={limit}",
                json=body,
            )
            return data.get("items", [])
        except Exception as e:
            logging.error("Search failed for %s + %s: %s", company_name, title_keywords, e)

# Dream 200 — List Analysis (2026-07-21)

> Source: Google Sheet from Alok/Cozmo ("Dream 200" tab, 223 companies). Scored 2026-07-21 by a 24-agent web-check sweep + follow-up pass (all 223 covered). Master file: `dream200-scored.csv`. Decision-maker sampling: `dm-sample` via Unipile classic search (Nitin's account; no Sales Nav on any connected account — counts are first-50-results floors, not totals).

## What the sheet is
Hand-curated (NOT scraped) target list, 7 columns (Company, Type, Sub-segment, HQ, Footprint, Website, Notes). Two halves:
- **125 P&C claims services** — 75 IA/CAT firms (independent adjusting), 21 TPAs/claims managers, plus flood servicers, managed-repair networks, inspection networks.
- **98 restoration operators** — 21 franchise networks (SERVPRO 2,350+, PuroClean 500+…), 41 regional contractors, 16 national contractors, contents/member networks.
Notes column carries insider intel (tech stacks, PE owners, named CIOs, "CAUTION" flags) — clearly written by someone who knows the industry. Zero dupes, zero missing websites.

## Verdict: strong list, three caveats
1. **Quality: high.** Curation shows real market knowledge; urgency signals annotated; even a competitor-conflict flag (Eberl).
2. **Caveat — IA-heavy:** 75 of 125 claims rows are IA/CAT adjusting firms. Mostly 11–50-person shops = mid-market Lane A at best, not the $1M TPA whales. The true TPA/claims-mgmt cluster (the "spending $2–3M" profile from the call) is only ~25–30 companies.
3. **Caveat — it's a 223, not a 200,** and ~38% scored C/X (small boutiques, homeowner-direct brands, niche contents/textile specialists). The working list is the **136 A+B companies**.
4. **Missing segment:** zero carriers (consistent with the TPA-first wedge — fine for now).

## Fit results (all 223 scored)
| Tier | Count | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| A | 28 | Dream: volume + urgency + reachable P&L owner |
| B | 108 | Strong fit, smaller contract |
| C | 85 | Marginal: tiny/niche/homeowner-direct |
| X | 2 | Excluded: Eberl (exclusive Wilbur license + Bees360/e360 = competitor-committed), Insurance Placement Solutions (adjuster-staffing model = displaced, not buyer) |

Lane split: 121 Lane A (claims side), 88 Lane B (restoration), 11 both, 3 none.

**Top A-tier by lane:** Lane A — Alacrity (post-restructuring modernization mandate), Davies NA, North American Risk Services (24/7 in-house FNOL), Team Focus (1M+ calls/yr), Alternative Claims Services (1,700+ adjuster roster, Citizens), National Flood Services, Engle Martin, McLarens, Pilot CAT, RYZE (Bain), Allcat, Colonial Claims, CNC, Accuserve. Lane B — SERVPRO, Paul Davis, PuroClean, DKI (own FNOL center), CORE Group, BELFOR, ATI (peer-CTO opening), BluSky, First Onsite (central estimation desk), Cotton Holdings (hiring AI role, named CIO), Kustom US, American Restoration, Phoenix Restoration, RestoPros.

## Decision-maker sampling (14 companies, empirical)
Method: Unipile classic people-search per company, first 50 results, count profiles whose headline shows the company + a decision-maker title (CEO/COO/President/Owner/VP/Director/GM). These are FLOORS (first page only).
| Segment | Sampled | Avg DMs found (first 50) |
|---|---|---|
| TPA / claims mgmt | Alacrity, NARS, Davies, Team Focus | **~9** |
| IA / CAT firms | Pilot, Wardlaw, Engle Martin, RYZE | **~4** |
| Restoration national | SERVPRO*, ATI, BluSky, First Onsite | **~19** |
| Restoration regional | Jenkins, RMC | **~8** |

*SERVPRO corporate looked low (4) because its 2,350 franchise OWNERS live under "SERVPRO of [City]" entities — the franchise-owner long tail is thousands of additional Lane B buyers not counted here.

## Audience math for Snowball outreach
- Across all 223: ~2,000 reachable decision-makers (floor). Matches/tops Alok's own 1,000–2,000 estimate.
- **Working audience (A+B only, 136 companies): ~1,200–1,400 decision-makers.** That's the DM + engagement universe.
- Franchise-owner expansion (SERVPRO/PuroClean/Rainbow etc. unit owners) adds thousands more for Lane B velocity deals — separate motion, separate list.

## Build plan
1. Scrape DM profiles for the 28 A-tier first (~250–300 people), then B-tier (~900–1,100). Store in the outreach targets DB with tier + lane + urgency note from `dream200-scored.csv`.
2. Multi-thread per company (CEO+COO+VPs); Alok's rule: one person's no ≠ company no unless CEO.
3. Engagement engine follows the same list (comment on their posts before DMing).
4. Respect X-tier: never contact Eberl or IPS from Cozmo-linked profiles.

    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, context=CTX, timeout=30) as r: return r.read().decode("utf-8","ignore")

# Alok Intake Questionnaire — DM-agent knowledge gaps (2026-07-22)

> Purpose: train the DM reply agent to answer queries + handle objections without Alok stepping in. Every question is closed-ended (yes/no, A-or-B, or one number). Built after scraping the full site (`website-scrape-2026-07-22.md`) — we only ask what the site + call + posts do NOT answer.
> WhatsApp-ready version at bottom. Answers get folded into `offer-facts.md` (to create) which becomes the DM agent's fact base.

## Why each question exists (internal notes — do NOT send)
- Q1–5 pricing: job post says $1–4K/mo restoration; call says $50–60K TPA land. Can the agent QUOTE these, or never name price?
- Q6–7 CTA: site has "Cozmo calls you in 60 seconds" widget + demo booking. Which is the DM conversion point?
- Q8–11 proof: which claims are DM-safe (Allianz is uncorroborated; case studies on site are fintech-era; mega-customer is NDA).
- Q12–13 compliance: site displays SOC 2 Type I AND Type II; call said "getting SOC certifications" — agent must not overclaim to a risk-savvy buyer.
- Q14–18 product limits: what NOT to promise (ESX files? commercial large-loss? auto? outbound marketing calls?).
- Q19–22 sales process: who takes the meeting, minimum deal, geography.
- Q23–25 agent rules: competitor name (still garbled from transcript!), no-go accounts, tone.

---

## THE QUESTIONNAIRE (send this)

*Pricing (answer with a number or one word)*
1. Restoration plan: can we quote "$1K–$4K/month" in DMs — yes or no?
2. If no: is the rule "never name a price, book the call" — yes or no?
3. TPA/carrier deals: is the typical starting workflow still $50–60K — yes or no?
4. Pilot: paid or free?
5. Contracts: monthly or annual for restoration? Monthly or annual for TPAs?

*Conversion (one word each)*
6. DM goal: book a demo with you, or push the "Cozmo calls you in 60 seconds" widget first?
7. The "spot the AI in 90 seconds or we don't deploy" line: safe to use in DMs — yes or no?

*Proof we're allowed to use (yes/no each)*
8. "2M+ production calls / 10M+ interactions" — usable?
9. "Allianz early partner" — usable in DMs?
10. "Two of the top five US restoration franchises onboarding" — usable?
11. The seven-figure customer: is "a top-2 player in its category" the exact phrase you want, or softer ("a leading claims company")?
12. The fintech-era case studies on the site (bank support 70%, collections 78%, motor FNOL): usable with P&C prospects, or hide them?

*Compliance (one word each)*
13. SOC 2 Type I: attained or in progress? Type II: attained or in progress?
14. US data residency: available today — yes or no?
15. Do you hold (or need) any state TPA/adjuster licenses — yes, no, or not applicable?

*What NOT to promise (yes/no each)*
16. Estimates: does Cozmo write actual Xactimate/Symbility files (ESX), or "carrier-ready scope language" only?
17. Commercial large-loss claims: in scope or out?
18. Auto claims: in scope or out (site says property)?
19. Outbound sales/marketing calls for restoration clients: offered or intake-only?
20. On escalation: does the human fallback come from THEIR team or does Cozmo provide 24/7 humans?

*Sales process (one word each)*
21. First meeting: always you, or can Nuha/someone else take it?
22. Geography for new leads: US-only, or US + Middle East?
23. Perils: water/fire/storm only, or all property perils?

*Agent rules*
24. The competitor you mentioned on our call (sounded like "Fatality") — please type the exact spelling.
25. Besides Eberl, any companies or people we must NEVER DM — yes (send names) or no?

---

# Documentation Lookup

Retrieve current documentation and code examples for any library using the Context7 CLI.

Make sure the CLI is up to date before running commands:

```bash
npm install -g ctx7@latest
```

Or run directly without installing:

```bash
npx ctx7@latest <command>
```

## Workflow

Two-step process: resolve the library name to an ID, then query docs with that ID.

```bash
# Step 1: Resolve library ID
ctx7 library <name> <query>

# Step 2: Query documentation
ctx7 docs <libraryId> <query>
```

You MUST call `ctx7 library` first to obtain a valid library ID UNLESS the user explicitly provides a library ID in the format `/org/project` or `/org/project/version`.

IMPORTANT: Do not run these commands more than 3 times per question. If you cannot find what you need after 3 attempts, use the best result you have.

## Step 1: Resolve a Library

Resolves a package/product name to a Context7-compatible library ID and returns matching libraries.

```bash
ctx7 library react "How to clean up useEffect with async operations"
ctx7 library nextjs "How to set up app router with middleware"
ctx7 library prisma "How to define one-to-many relations with cascade delete"
```

Always pass a `query` argument — it is required and directly affects result ranking. Use the user's intent to form the query, which helps disambiguate when multiple libraries share a similar name. Do not include any sensitive or confidential information such as API keys, passwords, credentials, personal data, or proprietary code in your query.

### Result fields

Each result includes:

- **Library ID** — Context7-compatible identifier (format: `/org/project`)
- **Name** — Library or package name
- **Description** — Short summary
- **Code Snippets** — Number of available code examples
- **Source Reputation** — Authority indicator (High, Medium, Low, or Unknown)
- **Benchmark Score** — Quality indicator (100 is the highest score)
- **Versions** — List of versions if available. Use one of those versions if the user provides a version in their query. The format is `/org/project/version`.

### Selection process

1. Analyze the query to understand what library/package the user is looking for
2. Select the most relevant match based on:
   - Name similarity to the query (exact matches prioritized)
   - Description relevance to the query's intent
   - Documentation coverage (prioritize libraries with higher Code Snippet counts)
   - Source reputation (consider libraries with High or Medium reputation more authoritative)
   - Benchmark score (higher is better, 100 is the maximum)
3. If multiple good matches exist, acknowledge this but proceed with the most relevant one
4. If no good matches exist, clearly state this and suggest query refinements
5. For ambiguous queries, request clarification before proceeding with a best-guess match

### Version-specific IDs

If the user mentions a specific version, use a version-specific library ID:

```bash
# General (latest indexed)
ctx7 docs /vercel/next.js "How to set up app router"

# Version-specific
ctx7 docs /vercel/next.js/v14.3.0-canary.87 "How to set up app router"
```

The available versions are listed in the `ctx7 library` output. Use the closest match to what the user specified.

## Step 2: Query Documentation

Retrieves up-to-date documentation and code examples for the resolved library.

```bash
ctx7 docs /facebook/react "How to clean up useEffect with async operations"
ctx7 docs /vercel/next.js "How to add authentication middleware to app router"
ctx7 docs /prisma/prisma "How to define one-to-many relations with cascade delete"
```

### Writing good queries

The query directly affects the quality of results. Be specific and include relevant details. Do not include any sensitive or confidential information such as API keys, passwords, credentials, personal data, or proprietary code in your query.

| Quality | Example |
|---------|---------|
| Good | `"How to set up authentication with JWT in Express.js"` |
| Good | `"React useEffect cleanup function with async operations"` |
| Bad | `"auth"` |
| Bad | `"hooks"` |

Use the user's full question as the query when possible, vague one-word queries return generic results.

The output contains two types of content: **code snippets** (titled, with language-tagged blocks) and **info snippets** (prose explanations with breadcrumb context).

## Authentication

Works without authentication. For higher rate limits:

```bash
# Option A: environment variable
export CONTEXT7_API_KEY=your_key

# Option B: OAuth login
ctx7 login
```

## Error Handling

If a command fails with a quota error ("Monthly quota reached" or "quota exceeded"):
1. Inform the user their Context7 quota is exhausted
2. Suggest they authenticate for higher limits: `ctx7 login`
3. If they cannot or choose not to authenticate, answer from training knowledge and clearly note it may be outdated

Do not silently fall back to training data — always tell the user why Context7 was not used.

## Common Mistakes

- Library IDs require a `/` prefix — `/facebook/react` not `facebook/react`
- Always run `ctx7 library` first — `ctx7 docs react "hooks"` will fail without a valid ID
- Use descriptive queries, not single words — `"React useEffect cleanup function"` not `"hooks"`
- Do not include sensitive information (API keys, passwords, credentials) in queries

content.content:
### Create Client Secret Request

Source: https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/realtime/subresources/client_secrets/methods/create

Use this cURL command to create a client secret. Specify the expiration time and session details like model and instructions.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.openai.com/v1/realtime/client_secrets \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "expires_after": {
      "anchor": "created_at",
      "seconds": 600
    },
    "session": {
      "type": "realtime",
      "model": "gpt-realtime",
      "instructions": "You are a friendly assistant."
    }
  }'
```

--------------------------------

### Create Session

Source: https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/realtime/subresources/sessions/methods/create

Creates an ephemeral API token for client-side applications. This token can be used to authenticate browser clients for the Realtime API and is configured with session parameters.

```APIDOC
## POST /realtime/sessions

### Description
Creates an ephemeral API token for use in client-side applications with the Realtime API. Can be configured with the same session parameters as the `session.update` client event. It responds with a session object, plus a `client_secret` key which contains a usable ephemeral API token that can be used to authenticate browser clients for the Realtime API.

### Method
POST

### Endpoint
/realtime/sessions

### Parameters
#### Request Body
- **client_secret** (object) - Ephemeral key returned by the API.
  - **expires_at** (number) - Timestamp for when the token expires. Currently, all tokens expire after one minute. format: unixtime
  - **value** (string) - Ephemeral key usable in client environments to authenticate connections to the Realtime API. Use this in client-side environments rather than a standard API token, which should only be used server-side.
- **input_audio_format** (string) - optional - The format of input audio. Options are `pcm16`, `g711_ulaw`, or `g711_alaw`.
- **input_audio_transcription** (object) - optional - Configuration for input audio transcription, defaults to off and can be set to `null` to turn off once on. Input audio transcription is not native to the model, since the model consumes audio directly. Transcription runs asynchronously and should be treated as rough guidance rather than the representation understood by the model.
  - **model** (string) - optional - The model to use for transcription.
- **instructions** (string) - optional - The default system instructions (i.e. system message) prepended to model calls. This field allows the client to guide the model on desired responses. The model can be instructed on response content and format, (e.g. “be extremely succinct”, “act friendly”, “here are examples of good responses”) and on audio behavior (e.g. “talk quickly”, “inject emotion into your voice”, “laugh frequently”). The instructions are not guaranteed to be followed by the model, but they provide guidance to the model on the desired behavior. Note that the server sets default instructions which will be used if this field is not set and are visible in the `session.created` event at the start of the session.
- **max_response_output_tokens** (number or "inf") - optional - Maximum number of output tokens for a single assistant response, inclusive of tool calls. Provide an integer between 1 and 4096 to limit output tokens, or `inf` for the maximum available tokens for a given model. Defaults to `inf`.
- **modalities** (array of "text" or "audio") - optional - The set of modalities the model can respond with. To disable audio, set this to [“text”].
- **output_audio_format** (string) - optional - The format of output audio. Options are `pcm16`, `g711_ulaw`, or `g711_alaw`.
- **prompt** (object) - optional - Reference to a prompt template and its variables. Learn more.
  - **id** (string) - The unique identifier of the prompt template to use.
  - **variables** (map) - optional - Optional map of values to substitute in for variables in your prompt. The substitution values can either be strings, or other Response input types like images or files.
    - **(string)** - The text input to the model.
    - **type**: "input_text" - The type of the input item. Always `input_text`.
    - **detail**: "low" or "high" or "auto" or "original" - The detail level of the image to be sent to the model. One of `high`, `low`, `auto`, or `original`. Defaults to `auto`.
    - **type**: "input_image" - The type of the input item. Always `input_image`.
    - **file_id** (string) - optional - The ID of the file to be sent to the model.
    - **image_url** (string) - optional - The URL of the image to be sent to the model. A fully qualified URL or base64 encoded image in a data URL. format: uri
    - **type**: "input_file" - The type of the input item. Always `input_file`.
    - **detail**: "low" or "high" - optional - The detail level of the file to be sent to the model. Use `low` for the default rendering behavior, or `high` to render the file at higher quality. Defaults to `low`.
    - **file_data** (string) - optional - The content of the file to be sent to the model.
    - **file_id** (string) - optional - The ID of the file to be sent to the model.
    - **file_url** (string) - optional - The URL of the file to be sent to the model. format: uri
    - **filename** (string) - optional - The name of the file to be sent to the model.
  - **version** (string) - optional - Optional version of the prompt template.
- **speed** (number) - optional

### Response
#### Success Response (200)
- **session object** - Returns the created Realtime session object.
- **client_secret** (object) - Contains a usable ephemeral API token.
  - **expires_at** (number) - Timestamp for when the token expires.
  - **value** (string) - Ephemeral key usable in client environments to authenticate connections to the Realtime API.

#### Response Example
{
  "session": {
    "id": "sess_abc123",
    "created_at": 1678886400,
    "expires_at": 1678886460,
    "parameters": {
      "model": "gpt-4",
      "instructions": "You are a helpful assistant."
    }
  },
  "client_secret": {
    "expires_at": 1678886460,
    "value": "sk-ephemeral-xyz789"
  }
}
```

--------------------------------

### Realtime Session Configuration

Source: https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/realtime/subresources/client_secrets

This section describes the parameters that can be configured when creating or managing a Realtime API session. These parameters control various aspects of the session, from speech detection to model behavior and audio output.

```APIDOC
## Realtime Session Configuration

This section describes the parameters that can be configured when creating or managing a Realtime API session. These parameters control various aspects of the session, from speech detection to model behavior and audio output.

### Parameters

#### Server-side VAD (Voice Activity Detection)

- **server_vad**: (object) - Optional. Configuration for server-side VAD.
  - **threshold**: (number) - Optional. Activation threshold for VAD (0.0 to 1.0). Defaults to 0.5. Higher values require louder audio.
  - **duration**: (number) - Optional. Duration of silence to detect speech stop (in milliseconds). Defaults to 500ms.

#### Semantic VAD

- **semantic_vad**: (object) - Optional. Configuration for server-side semantic turn detection.
  - **type**: ("semantic_vad") - Required. Type of turn detection.
  - **create_response**: (boolean) - Optional. Whether to automatically generate a response when a VAD stop event occurs.
  - **eagerness**: ("low" | "medium" | "high" | "auto") - Optional. The eagerness of the model to respond. Defaults to "auto".
  - **interrupt_response**: (boolean) - Optional. Whether to automatically interrupt any ongoing response when a VAD start event occurs.

#### Output Configuration

- **output**: (object) - Optional. Configuration for the output audio.
  - **format**: (RealtimeAudioFormats) - Optional. The format of the output audio.
  - **speed**: (number) - Optional. The speed of the model’s spoken response. Minimum 0.25, maximum 1.5. 1.0 is the default.
  - **voice**: (string) - Optional. The voice the model uses to respond. Cannot be changed after the first audio response. Recommended voices: `marin`, `cedar`.
    Possible values: "alloy", "ash", "ballad", "coral", "echo", "sage", "shimmer", "verse", "marin", "cedar".

#### Session and Model Settings

- **expires_at**: (number) - Optional. Expiration timestamp for the session, in seconds since epoch.
- **include**: (array of string) - Optional. Additional fields to include in server outputs. Example: `["item.input_audio_transcription.logprobs"]`.
- **instructions**: (string) - Optional. Default system instructions to guide the model's responses and audio behavior.
- **max_output_tokens**: (number | "inf") - Optional. Maximum number of output tokens for a single assistant response. Defaults to `inf`.
- **model**: (string) - Optional. The Realtime model used for this session.
    Possible values: "gpt-realtime", "gpt-realtime-1.5", "gpt-realtime-2", "gpt-realtime-2025-08-28", "gpt-4o-realtime-preview", "gpt-4o-realtime-preview-2024-10-01", "gpt-4o-realtime-preview-2024-12-17", "gpt-4o-realtime-preview-2025-06-03", "gpt-4o-mini-realtime-preview", "gpt-4o-mini-realtime-preview-2024-12-17", "gpt-realtime-mini", "gpt-realtime-mini-2025-10-06", "gpt-realtime-mini-2025-12-15", "gpt-audio-1.5", "gpt-audio-mini", "gpt-audio-mini-2025-10-06", "gpt-audio-mini-2025-12-15".
```

### Realtime Session Creation Response

content.thinking:
Ansh is asking for three key improvements to the voice agent. First, questions should be more open-ended rather than strictly yes/no, allowing Alok to provide richer responses. Second, the agent needs a warmer personality—cheerful and emotionally expressive with varied intonation and clear speech, which can be shaped through realtime instructions that direct tone and delivery.

For the voice itself, Marin (female) is recommended and should be kept with cheerful direction, though Cedar is another option. Third, the agent should actively probe answers—asking follow-up questions like "what do you mean?" or "can you give an example?"—until responses are actionable and sufficient.

Now I'm reviewing the current question set to identify gaps. The existing 25 questions cover pricing, pilot terms, contract details, CTAs, guarantees, proof points, compliance requirements, scope limitations, and process details. I'm thinking through what else a DM reply agent would need to ask about.

There are several critical gaps: ROI economics (whether the $500→$60 cost-per-claim figure can be cited publicly), how to counter the "we already have an answering service" objection, what to say when prospects claim they've tried AI before and it failed, which integrations are actually live versus roadmap, who handles security questionnaires and whether there's a trust pack to send, whether referenceable customers exist, how persistent the agent can be with follow-ups, and what negotiation flexibility exists around discounts or free pilots.

On logistics: what length of initial call to promise in the DM (15 minutes?), tone boundaries for messaging as Alok, any seasonal urgency hooks that are approved, and whether the agent needs to handle non-English inbound messages.

Rather than expanding to 40 questions, I'm narrowing to the highest-impact ones: the public usability of that cost-per-claim metric, exactly which integrations are live today versus future, the best counter to "we already have an answering service," and the approved response to "we tried AI before and it failed."

Now I'm working through the reference customer policy, how many follow-up DMs before stopping, whether the agent can offer a free month or pilot to close the booking, and what initial meeting duration to promise. This brings the total to around 34 questions, which stretches the voice session to about 12 minutes. **Voice & delivery:** she's now directed to be cheerful and expressive — audible smile, varied intonation, human reactions ("oh nice," a light laugh), podcast-host energy, never survey-robot. # Cozmo — How the Product Actually Works (DM-agent grade)

> Distilled 2026-07-22 from the full site scrape (15 pages incl. /platform), the onboarding call, and the YC job post. This is the MECHANICS layer. The PERMISSIONS layer (what we may claim/quote) comes from Alok's intake answers → `offer-facts.md`.

## The one-sentence product
AI employees that run a property insurance claim end to end — answer the call, read the documents, apply the client's rules, dispatch the crew, write the estimate, file the FNOL with the carrier, drive it to settlement — inside the client's existing systems, with every action logged to an audit trail.

## The 7-step loop (their own /platform framing)
1. **Answer** — picks up every inbound call 24/7 (voice/chat/WhatsApp/email; 110+ languages; 850ms latency; callers can interrupt naturally; 85–90% can't tell it's AI). Captures the loss in the caller's own words as a structured record.
2. **Read** — ingests the policy, damage photos, videos, documents. Vision agent: reads dashcam/CCTV, pulls damage indicators from photos, links evidence to the right claim, guides the customer to capture the right photos first time.
3. **Decide** — applies the client's own rules deterministically ("does not guess approvals"; same inputs → same outcome; every decision traceable to a specific rule). Regional rule packs (US/EU/UAE/KSA). PII redacted at token level.
4. **Dispatch** — checks technician availability, dispatches the crew (45-min avg on-site response claim), texts the work authorization for one-tap signing. Direct dispatch into **Encircle, Dash, Albiware, ServiceTitan**.
5. **Estimate** — builds carrier-ready estimates from the field documentation, with **Xactimate/Symbility scope language** (whether actual files or language-only = intake Q16).
6. **File** — files the FNOL with the carrier in the carrier-required format, same night, and tracks claim status through carrier portals.
7. **Settle** — drives to resolution/payment, full audit trail exportable for adjusters/regulators.

## The architecture (why it's not "a voice bot")
- **APE (Agent Protocol Engine)** — the control layer: coordinates voice/vision/skills agents over ONE shared structured state, enforces policy continuously, keeps the regulatory audit trail. Their claim: no prompt-dependence, deterministic guardrails.
- **One conversation across channels** — a claim can start on a call, continue on WhatsApp, finish on web without restarting; the agent already knows what was said.
- **Human escalation** — only when judgment is needed (big payouts, fraud, hardship); the human gets the full prepared case. Fallback humans = the client's own team (their FAQ; confirm Q20).
- **Writes back to the system of record** (Guidewire-class core systems named) — "no rip and replace"; sits over existing telephony (carrier-grade SIP, in-country numbers in 80+ countries).
- **Analytics layer** — 50+ metrics, every conversation scored, latency broken down by pipeline stage, full API.
- **The claims desk** — client-facing console: live worklist ("needs a person: 6"), SLA clocks per stage, approvals queue.

## The economics story (per buyer)
- **TPA/carrier:** cost per claim ~$500 human → ~$60 Cozmo (Alok's call number; written-use pending Q26). Site: 70% lower cost per successful resolution. Outcome-based pricing: "you pay when a claim resolves — a call that goes nowhere costs you nothing." Margin math: TPAs run 10–20% margins; 1 point of efficiency = 10 points of margin.
- **Restoration:** never miss a 2am call (job goes to whoever answers first); crew dispatched + work auth signed by text in ~90 seconds; FNOL filed same night = paid faster. Flat monthly by call volume ($1–4K/mo per job post; quotability pending Q1). Live in ~7 business days.
- **Speed as proof:** 3-week pilot→production (carriers); "what their prior vendor did in 8 months we showed in 2 hours" (Memphis story).

## The demo asset (critical for DMs)
The site widget: **"Drop your number and Cozmo calls you in under a minute. Ask it anything a policyholder with a 2am loss would."** Plus the FAQ guarantee: "If you can spot the AI in the first ninety seconds, we will not deploy."
→ The DM "demo link" isn't a video — it's hellocozmo.ai where THE PRODUCT ITSELF CALLS THE PROSPECT in 60 seconds. Self-demonstrating. (Default CTA vs calendar = intake Q6.)

## DM conversation architecture (Ansh's flow, sharpened per lane)
**Lane A — TPA / IA / claims execs:**
1. Connect on common ground (their post, industry event, PE pressure, cat season).
2. Discovery Q: "How are you handling claims intake right now — and do you know your cost per successful resolution?" (their vocabulary: cost per claim, cycle time, SLA breaches, book of claims).
3. The hook: the $500→$60 gap [pending Q26] or "70% lower cost per resolution, live in 3 weeks, you pay only when a claim resolves."
4. The ask: 60-second widget call OR 10-minute meeting [pending Q6/Q33].
**Lane B — restoration owners:**
2'. Discovery Q: "Who answers your phones at 2am? How many jobs went to whoever picked up first last storm?"
3'. Hook: every call answered live, crew dispatched + work auth signed in 90 seconds, FNOL filed same night, flat monthly fee, live in a week.

## What we still do NOT know (by design — the intake covers it)
Pricing quotability (Q1–3), pilot paid/free (Q4), contract terms (Q5), CTA default (Q6), which proof claims are cleared (Q7–12), SOC 2 truth (Q13), Xactimate files vs language (Q16), scope edges (Q17–19), integrations live-vs-roadmap (Q27), objection counters in his words (Q28–29), reference policy (Q30), persistence + incentives + meeting ask (Q31–33), never-say list (Q34), competitor name (Q24).
**Nothing in the DM flow should ship until those answers land.**
